defaultStrategy turns the check off for the columns it covers; only 'null' and constant keep it safe, since they discard whatever a new column holds. To make a database refuse unmasked rows altogether, set requireMasking on its alias.

docs.title: Generate data
docs.text:
Some tables can't be copied at all, even masked, and a new system may have no production data yet. synthesize fills existing tables with generated rows, using nothing but the target's own catalog:

bauta synthesize --connection staging --table customers:1000 --table orders:5000 --dry-run
bauta synthesize --connection staging --table customers:1000 --table orders:5000 --yes

customers: 1000 row(s)
  id                           primary key  sequential, from 1
  email                        name         an email address at example.test
  first_name                   name         a first name
  phone                        name         digits shaped like +1 555 010 0000
  birth_date                   name         a birth date between 1940 and 2004
  balance                      type         a decimal with 2 places, sometimes NULL
  sample: {'id': 1, 'email': 'u5e9bbb2e91df@example.test', 'first_name': 'Hugo', ...}
  • Keys are unique. Integer keys continue after the table's maximum, text keys run S1, S2, ... (zero-padded in a fixed-width column), and UUID keys are generated.
  • Values continue between runs. Generators are indexed by row number, counted from the rows already there, so a second run doesn't repeat or collide with the first.
  • Foreign keys resolve. Values are drawn from the parent's rows, and parents are filled first, whatever the --table order. A table keyed only by foreign keys gets as many rows as its parents allow.
  • Names drive realism. Columns named like personal data get realistic values, by the rules discover uses (your own included). Everything else is random within its type, dates from 2015 to the end of this year. Nullable columns are NULL about one time in ten.
  • Reproducible. The same --seed on the same starting tables makes the same rows (within a calendar year, as the date span grows each January).
  • CHECK constraints are kept where they list values (status IN (...)) or bound a number (amount > 0 AND amount < 1000). Any other check, such as start_date <= end_date, is named as synthesize starts, since rows breaking it will be refused.

docs.title: Shaped like production: --profile
docs.text:
bauta synthesize --connection staging --table orders:50000 --profile production --dry-run

--profile ALIAS shapes the rows like the same table in another connection: each column NULL as often, numbers and dates within the same range, and a column of few values (status, region) taking each label as often. Only aggregates are read, never a row:

  • columns named like personal data, and keys, are never read;
  • labels come only from columns of at most 20 values, and only those at least 5 rows share, so a value rare enough to point at someone is never copied;
  • a number's or date's extremes are read, so leave out a column whose extremes are sensitive, or name it in your own rules.

A CHECK takes precedence over the profile, and the profile over names. --dry-run shows which each column follows. - --rows sets the count for any --table given without one. Nothing is written without --yes.

Limits: a table referencing itself through a NOT NULL column can't be filled (a nullable self-reference is left NULL). A non-key UNIQUE column is satisfied only where its type has room: a name or short code can repeat, and the database's refusal says how many rows were already committed. Even with --profile, columns are shaped one by one, with no correlations between them. Tables must exist first; schema creates them.

docs.title: Keep a masking manifest
docs.text:
With manifest set in jobs.yaml, each run writes a sealed record of what was masked, how, and under which key fingerprint: a file, replaced by each run, or a table, which keeps every run's. It's what an auditor asks for.

With run --job, as an orchestrator's task per job runs, a file isn't replaced: each run merges its jobs in under a lock, replacing only their own entries, and re-seals it. What the file held must verify first; one that doesn't is never overwritten, and the run logs what it did:

  • Altered, or unreadable: it is moved aside as manifest.json.rejected-<time>, and started afresh.
  • Signed with a key the run can't check (another key, or none set): a task set up wrong, so the file is kept and the run's manifest written beside it as manifest.json.unmerged-<time>.

A file is always replaced in one step, never read half-written.

manifest: ../transaction/manifest.json   # a file, relative to jobs.yaml
manifest:
  connection: warehouse                  # or a table

bauta verify-manifest                    # the latest; exit 0 intact, 1 altered
bauta verify-manifest --run RUN_ID       # an earlier one, from a table

--manifest FILE or --manifest-connection ALIAS overrides the setting, on run and on verify-manifest. Set BAUTA_MANIFEST_KEY to sign manifests; only a signature shows who wrote one. The manifest describes its content and how verification works.

docs.title: What it records
docs.text:
{
  "generatedAt": "2026-09-16T13:25:57+00:00",
  "runId": "0b6c1f0e-4d1e-4f7a-9a43-2f0c9f6a1d52",
  "jobs": [
    {
      "job": "maskCustomers",
      "status": "completed",
      "sourceConnection": "prod",
      "targetConnection": "staging",
      "targetTable": "customers",
      "keyFingerprint": "d5930cf83dea",
      "rowCount": 48210,
      "columns": [
        {"column": "id", "strategy": "key", "domain": "customer", "source": "column"},
        {"column": "notes", "strategy": "null", "domain": null, "source": "column"}
      ]
    }
  ],
  "maskedBy": "bauta-rs/0.1.3",
  "tool": {"name": "bauta", "version": "0.1.3"},
  "configuration": {"jobsFile": "configuration/jobs.yaml", "sha256": "9f2c…"},
  "integrity": {
    "algorithm": "sha256",
    "digest": "4be1…",
    "signatureAlgorithm": "hmac-sha256",
    "signature": "0c7a…",
    "signingKeyFingerprint": "71d04ab2e913"
  }
}
  • columns lists the columns the query actually returned, and the policy applied to each. source says whether a column was listed in columns or fell to defaultStrategy.
  • A masked job that failed or was skipped is still listed, with its status and no columns. "This copy was not refreshed" belongs in the record too.
  • The manifest is written even when the run fails. It never contains a value or the key.
  • configuration names the jobs file and its SHA-256, so a reviewer can tell which policy produced the run, and includes each included file with its own.
  • maskedBy is python, or the native masker and its version.
  • runId matches the run's history. After run --job, each job's entry carries its own runId, generatedAt and maskedBy.

From Python, RunResult.maskingManifest(jobsFile.jobs) returns the manifest before sealing, without tool, configuration or integrity; sealManifest adds the last.

docs.title: In a table
docs.text:
To keep every run's manifest, or keep them with the data they describe, store them in a table:

manifest:
  connection: warehouse         # an alias in connections.yaml
  table: audit.bauta_manifest   # optional; bauta_manifest by default

or --manifest-connection ALIAS for one run. Each is stored as the file would be, in 2000-character pieces so one table definition fits every database, under its run id. The table must exist first (tables).

bauta verify-manifest with no file reads the latest manifest from there, and --run RUN_ID picks an earlier one.

The table is not what makes a manifest trustworthy. Whoever can write to it can replace a manifest, and recompute its digest to match. Only a signature shows who wrote one, wherever it's stored.

docs.title: Sealing and verifying
docs.text:
Every manifest carries a SHA-256 digest of its content, showing it hasn't been edited; but anyone can recompute a digest. To show who wrote it, set a signing key, and it is also signed with HMAC-SHA256:

export BAUTA_MANIFEST_KEY=...      # at least 16 characters; not the masking key
bauta run

bauta verify-manifest       # the manifest jobs.yaml names; or a FILE, or --manifest-connection ALIAS

verify-manifest exits 0 for an intact manifest (saying whether it was signed), and 1 if it was altered or its signature doesn't match. With BAUTA_MANIFEST_KEY set, an unsigned manifest exits 1 too, or an edit could pass by dropping the signature. Verifying a signed manifest without its key exits 2. --manifest-key-variable reads the key from another variable.

docs.title: Keep joins intact
docs.text:
Every mask is derived from the key, a domain, and the value itself:

mask = strategy( HMAC(key, domain, value) )

The same value in the same domain masks the same way in every table and on every run, so a join survives masking when both sides share a domain and a strategy:

# customers
id:          { strategy: key, domain: customer }
# orders
customer_id: { strategy: key, domain: customer }

The domain defaults to the column's lower-cased name, so email in two tables agrees already; set domain where the two sides are named differently.

Masks depend on nothing but the value, key and domain, not row order or a seed, so a rerun or next week's incremental load gives the same values. shuffle, which depends on how rows fall into chunks, is the exception.

Numbers are keyed on their decimal text, so an id read as an int, a Decimal or '42' masks alike under hash. key keeps its input's type, so keep one type per domain, or give it normalize: [integer].

docs.title: Make it faster
docs.text:
Three things decide how fast a job moves rows, in this order.

The masking policy, by about fivefold. key is expensive because it must be a permutation; hash hides as much for a thirtieth of the work wherever a column needn't stay one-to-one. See speed.

The native masker, about ten times faster on the same policy, with identical results. On a wide table, where masking sets the pace, it can also spread each chunk over several cores (maskingThreads).

chunkSize, for latency rather than throughput. Locally, chunks from 500 to 200,000 rows finish the same job within 7% of each other. What a chunk costs is a round trip: 25 ms away, a million rows take 123 seconds at chunkSize: 500 and 8.8 at 10000. Latency stops mattering once a chunk's masking outlasts its round trips:

chunkSize  >  2 x latency / per-row masking cost

That is a few thousand rows at 5 ms, about six thousand at 25 ms. Cheap policies need larger chunks, having less work to hide the wait behind.

To see which of these sets a job's pace, bauta history shows the seconds each run spent reading, masking and writing, and bauta bench measures reading and masking against your own source before anything is copied.

If a job is still slow, look at the database: the target's indexes and constraints during a bulk load, and a stage table (targetTableStage) so the final table is written once. And for one very large table, where one connection is the limit, read it as several partitions at once.

docs.title: What each strategy costs
docs.text:
A million rows of six columns plus a kept id (a reference, an integer, an email, a hex token, a session string, a phone number), SQLite to SQLite, with the native masker on one thread, on a ten-core M1 Pro. python benchmarks/masking.py measures it again (see benchmarks):

Policy Rows a second email, two hash, three keep 333,000 two key columns, email, two hash, digits 131,000 two fpe columns, email, two hash, digits 268,000 five key columns, one hash 74,000

key costs the most because it has to be a permutation: a Feistel network per value, about thirty times the work of hash's one digest. Where nothing joins on a column, hash hides as much far more cheaply. fpe is a permutation too, but FF1's ten AES rounds cost less natively than key's forty-odd digests.

Repeated values are remembered per column (up to 16,384 in Python, and 65,536 across chunks in the native masker for key, fpe and fake*), so foreign keys and low-cardinality columns mask many times faster.

docs.title: The native masker
docs.text:
bauta-rs is an optional extension that masks in Rust. It changes no result, and everything works without it. Install it as an extra:

pip install "bauta[native]"

Wheels are published for Linux (x86-64 and ARM, glibc 2.17 or newer) and macOS (Apple silicon and Intel), each covering every supported Python. Elsewhere pip compiles it, which needs Rust 1.83 or newer.

Only the matching version is used. bauta-rs is released with every bauta, and the extra pins the match. Another version is ignored, since two versions aren't certain to mask identically, and a difference would surface as joins that quietly stop matching. The manifest records which implementation masked.

Upgrading bauta alone leaves the extension behind, so a run with masked jobs stops before it starts, naming the version to install; requireNative: false or BAUTA_REQUIRE_NATIVE=0 masks in Python instead. Where the extension was never installed, or BAUTA_NATIVE=0, a run masks in Python and says so; requireNative: true stops it there too.

From a clone, pip install ./mask-rs/py builds the extension at the checkout's version.

It covers key, fpe, hash, email, digits, number, redact (but its custom patterns) and the fake* strategies, which is where the time goes. Everything else stays in Python: the already-cheap strategies, custom strategies, and values the extension doesn't handle (dates, UUIDs, non-ASCII text where characters matter), which are handed back one by one, so a value Python would refuse still refuses with the same message.

The second policy above, a million rows, SQLite to SQLite:

Masker Rows a second Python 13,600 Rust, one thread, reading, masking and writing in turn 100,000 Rust, one thread, overlapped with the database (the default) 132,000 Rust, maskingThreads: auto (5 threads) 329,000

The two implementations compute identical masks, a release requirement; see two implementations.

docs.title: Masking threads
docs.text:
The native masker can spread each chunk over several cores. Every mask depends on its value alone, so the result is identical for any number of threads; only the time changes. jobs.yaml's maskingThreads sets how many threads each job masks with:

maskingThreads Each job masks with Use it when 1 (default) One thread. You haven't measured a need, or the database shares the machine. A number, such as 4 That many threads, every job. You want a fixed share. It can't exceed the cores available: validate and run refuse it. auto Half the cores available, divided between the jobs running when it starts. Bauta has the machine to itself, and you want masking as fast as the job can use it.

Why half. Masking only has to keep up with reading and writing, which need cores of their own, as may the database. On a wide table on ten cores, four masking threads copied as fast as six or eight, and ten were slower than any.

How auto divides the cores. When a job starts, it gets half the cores ÷ jobs running, counting the jobs already running and those starting with it, and at least one. A running job keeps its share; cores freed later go to the next job to start. With workers: 2 on 8 cores, where a and b run together and c waits for both:

Job Starts Jobs running Threads a first 2 2 b with a 2 2 c once a and b finish 1 4

Cores available are the ones the process may use: on Linux, a container's CPU limit and CPU affinity, not the host's total; on macOS, the core count.

With partitions, slices may take over auto's threads: see partitions: auto.

A number applies to every job, not shared: workers: 4 with maskingThreads: 4 on 8 cores runs 16 masking threads. Only auto divides the cores.

BAUTA_MASKING_THREADS overrides the setting for one environment, as a number or auto, and is checked the same way.

What never uses more than one thread: masking without the extension (not installed, or BAUTA_NATIVE=0), and strategies the extension doesn't cover, such as shuffle, dateShift, redact with patterns, and your own.

Seeing what it chose. bauta validate prints the plan:

masking: bauta-rs 0.2.4, 2 to 5 thread(s) per job (maskingThreads: auto; 10 core(s)): 2 with 2 jobs running, 5 for a job running alone

and each masked job logs what it got as it starts:

maskCustomers: masking with 4 thread(s) (2 job(s) running, 8 core(s))

When it helps. Threads help where masking, not the database, sets the pace: wide tables with many masked columns. A million rows of 25 masked columns, SQLite to SQLite on ten cores, from the native-masking demo:

maskingThreads Rows a second 1 31,000 auto (5 threads) 106,000

A narrow table gains little, since its time goes to writing.

docs.title: Partitions
docs.text:
One job reads, masks and writes on one connection to each database, however large its table. partitions divides it into slices of a numeric column, each with connections and threads of its own, all loading the same table:

partitions:
  column: id
  count: 4

A masked swap copy, PostgreSQL to PostgreSQL in Docker on the job's ten-core machine, the second policy above, one masking thread per slice; every run wrote the same table, byte for byte:

Masker Partitions Time Rows a second native, 2,000,000 rows none 15.4 s 130,000 2 8.0 s 250,000 (1.9 times) 4 5.0 s 403,000 (3.1 times) 8 4.8 s 415,000 (3.2 times) Python, 300,000 rows none 25.4 s 11,800 4 25.0 s 12,000 (1.0 times)

Past four slices the machine had no cores left: the database server and the job shared the same ten. With the source, the target and the job on machines of their own, the ceiling is whichever of them runs out first.

It pays where the database waits, not where Python masks. Slices overlap their reading and writing, mostly waits on a socket. They are threads, and Python masking holds the interpreter lock, so without the native masker a masked job gains nothing, as the table shows.

Size it to the databases. Each slice is another connection to each, counted against maxConcurrentJobs; beyond what the servers serve at once, more slices only queue.

Partition on an indexed column that doesn't change, such as the primary key: each slice then reads only its range, and no row moves between slices while the job runs. Slices are as even as the column's values are spread.

docs.title: partitions: auto
docs.text:
Rather than choosing a column and a count for each job, let each job choose as it starts:

defaults:
  partitions: auto              # every job; or on one job, or {column: id, count: auto} to name the column

The column is the target table's primary key, where it is one numeric column the query returns: what a slice reads by range from an index, and what doesn't change while it does.

The count is the fewest of:

Limit Why The job's share of the cores: half of them, divided between the jobs running when it starts The same share maskingThreads: auto reckons, spent once -- see below The places its source and target connections have free (maxConcurrentJobs) Each slice opens a connection to each One slice per 250,000 rows, reckoned from the span of the key A small table gains less than another pair of connections costs One, for a masked job without the native masker Its slices would take turns at Python's interpreter lock, and gain nothing (the table above)

A job it can't slice is read as one stream, with a log line saying why: no single numeric primary key the query returns, a query SQL Server won't wrap (one holding WITH or ORDER BY), a SQLite target, or files and Iceberg. So auto never stops a job, and can sit under defaults.

With maskingThreads. Where maskingThreads: auto gave a job no more threads than it has slices, each slice masks on its own thread, so the job's share of the cores is spent once; with fewer slices than threads, the slices share the pool. A number set for maskingThreads is kept, and the slices share it.

The log says what each job chose and why:

partitions: reading events as 4 slices of id at once, set by its share of the cores (4)
partitions: reading customers as one stream: its target has no primary key to slice by

docs.title: Measure a job
docs.text:
bauta bench reads each job's query from its real source, transforms and masks it as run would, and writes nothing. It says how fast each stage went, and which one would set a run's pace:

bauta bench --job maskCustomers --rows 200000

masker: bauta-rs 0.2.4, 1 thread(s)
Reading and masking were measured in turn, and nothing was written. A run overlaps them, so whichever is slower sets its pace,
unless writing to the target is slower still.

JOB                                ROWS  CONNECT  READ ROWS/S  MASK ROWS/S  WAITED  SETS THE PACE
maskCustomers                  200,000+     0.04      412,000      134,000     0.0  masking

+ the query returns more rows than were read; --rows reads more.
  • --rows (default 100,000) is how many rows of each query to read, to the next whole chunk. A query that returns fewer is read whole, and its row count has no +.
  • --job names a job to measure, and repeats; without it, every active job is.
  • READ ROWS/S covers running the query and fetching its rows; MASK ROWS/S transforms and masking, on the threads a job running alone would get; CONNECT opening the connection.
  • It doesn't measure the write. Where reading and masking are fast but a run is slow, the target is the limit; bauta history shows its WRITE seconds.
  • An incremental job is read from its watermarkInitial, as its first run or a full refresh would read it. A job with partitions is read as one stream.
  • It reads production, as a run does, and the source's read limit applies: WAITED is seconds it held bench back. --format json gives the same as JSON, with the seconds of each stage.

It exits 1 if a job couldn't be measured, naming why, and measures the others.

docs.title: Limiting what a job reads
docs.text:
maxRowsReadPerSecond on a connection caps how many rows a second jobs read from it, all of them together:

production:
  type: postgresql
  ...
  maxRowsReadPerSecond: 50000
  • One budget for the connection, shared by every job and partition reading it, across processes: two jobs at once get about half each.
  • A chunk at a time. A job waits after each chunk for as long as its rows owe, so the rate holds over a few chunks; a pause earns at most a second's worth.
  • It holds back reading only. With the native masker, masking and writing go on during the wait, recorded as WAITED in history.
  • Sampling commands aren't limited (discover, audit --connect, coverage), nor are writes; bauta bench is.

Choose it from what the source can spare: a limit below what a job could read makes it take longer, by exactly WAITED.

docs.title: Mask a table
docs.text:
Masking is a stage of a data job: rows are masked as they stream from source to target, so unmasked data never reaches the target, not even a stage table.

extract (prod)  →  transform  →  mask  →  load (staging)

So masking gets the job's streaming, retries, watermarks, --dry-run and structured logs.

docs.title: A masked job
docs.text:
Add a masking section to any data job:

maskCustomers:
  active: true
  sourceConnection: prod
  sourceQuery: select * from customers
  targetConnection: staging
  targetTableFinal: customers
  insertStrategy: upsert
  chunkSize: 5000
  masking:
    key: ${MASKING_KEY}
    columns:
      id:          { strategy: key, domain: customer }
      email:       email
      phone:       { strategy: digits, keepLeading: 1 }
      full_name:   fakeName
      birth_date:  { strategy: dateShift, maxDays: 30 }
      notes:       'null'
      created_at:  keep
Field Required or default Meaning key required The secret every mask is derived from, from the environment. See the key. columns required Column name → policy: a strategy name, or a mapping with strategy, an optional domain, and the strategy's options. See strategies. defaultStrategy optional The policy for any column columns doesn't name. Leave it unset unless you mean it; see every column must be covered.

Masking applies to sourceQuery's result columns, after its transforms, matching names ignoring case. To mask values a database compares as equal alike (padded, or differing in case), give the strategy normalize. 'null' needs its quotes: a bare null in YAML means "no value". bauta validate checks the key, every strategy and every option, offline.

docs.title: The key
docs.text:
The key stops someone who knows this scheme from masking likely values (common names, every phone number in an area code) and matching them against the copy.

  • Read it from the environment, key: ${MASKING_KEY}, never with a ${NAME:-default}, and never commit it.
  • Make it random: python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))". At least 16 characters of 8 different ones are required, and validate warns below an estimated 128 bits (keys).
  • Rotating it changes every mask, so a copy masked under the old key won't join to one under the new. Each masked job records its key's fingerprint, and an upsert or append job whose key has changed stops the run, since its target still holds rows masked under the old key. A swap or overwrite job replaces its whole target and carries on. See rotating the masking key.
  • The key never appears in logs, errors or the manifest. Runs log its fingerprint instead, a short, non-reversible identifier: two runs with the same fingerprint used the same key.

Whoever holds the key can confirm a guess ("is this row Alice?") by masking it and comparing, so guard it like production credentials. The security model sets out what masking does and doesn't protect.

docs.title: Masking in place
docs.text:
To mask a table where it stands, make the source and target the same and load through a stage table:

maskCustomersInPlace:
  sourceConnection: staging
  sourceQuery: select * from customers
  targetConnection: staging
  targetTableStage: customers_masked_stage   # same shape, created beforehand
  targetTableFinal: customers
  insertStrategy: swap
  chunkSize: 5000
  masking: ...

Masked rows stream into the stage, which is then swapped with the original, so a run that fails first leaves the original untouched. Use swap, not upsert, if a key column is masked: an upsert matches by primary key, so a masked key would add rows rather than replace them.

A swap renames tables. Views follow, but other tables' foreign keys and PostgreSQL's materialized views don't (how a swap works), so copy a referenced table into a separate database instead; audit --connect reports a swap of one as an error.

docs.title: Propose a policy
docs.text:
bauta discover --connection prod --table customers --table orders --target staging --output proposal.yaml

For each table, discover reads the schema and samples rows (--sample, default 1000), then writes a jobs.yaml with a proposed policy for every column. Each proposal carries a comment saying what it was based on:

    masking:
      key: ${MASKING_KEY}
      columns:
        id: {strategy: keep}  # numeric key (domain customers); use key if the ids themselves are meaningful
        email: {strategy: email}  # name suggests an email address
        phone: {strategy: digits}  # name suggests a phone number
        notes: {strategy: 'null'}  # name suggests free text, which can hold PII anywhere
        status: {strategy: keep}  # no sign of personal data -- review
  • Names first, then values. Column names are matched against rules for common patterns (email, phone, SSN, card, name, address, birth date and so on). A name-based suggestion is dropped if it doesn't fit the column's type, so place_of_birth isn't treated as a date. Sampled values are then checked for emails, national identifiers, card numbers (with a Luhn check), IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, MAC addresses, UUIDs, dates, phone numbers and long free text.
  • Inside JSON documents. A JSON column is read key by key and path by path against the same rules, so {"contact": {"alt_email": ...}} is found and proposed as a json policy naming each path: {strategy: json, fields: {contact.alt_email: {strategy: email}}}.
  • Keys are decided together. Primary keys, the columns that foreign keys reference, and the foreign-key columns themselves get matching domains, so both ends of a relationship agree. Numeric keys are proposed as keep, since surrogate ids reveal little, and text keys as key. --mask-keys masks the numeric ones too, in the domain each relationship shares:
id: {strategy: key, domain: customers}          # --mask-keys
customer_id: {strategy: key, domain: customers} # the other end, same domain

Both ends move together, so references still match. Use it where the ids themselves are meaningful (sequential ids leak how many customers there are, and when each joined) or must not be production's. A masked primary key makes a later key rotation go through bauta clear (rotating the masking key). - Sampled values stay in memory. None of them is printed, logged or written. - Load settings. With a separate --target, jobs upsert and load parent tables before child tables. Without one, the proposal masks in place through a <table>_masked_stage swap. - A whole schema at once. --all-tables proposes for every table, and --schema NAME for another schema's. Pair it with bauta coverage, which fails on anything the jobs then leave out. - --output refuses to overwrite an existing file, so it can't replace a policy that has already been reviewed.

Treat the result as a starting point for review. It isn't a finished policy.

What every job shares is written once, under defaults: the connections, the insert strategy and the masking key, so each job holds only what a reviewer has to read, and no edit can leave one job under another key. To paste the jobs into a file with defaults of its own, pass --self-contained, which writes every setting into every job.

docs.title: Keeping a policy up to date
docs.text:
A column added to or dropped from production stops every job reading it, since every column must be covered. discover --update runs each masked job's query and reports both, proposing a policy for each new column:

$ bauta discover --update
maskCustomers (configuration/jobs.d/crm.yaml):
  + ssn: {strategy: key}  # name suggests a government identifier; key keeps it unique and shaped
  + home_email: {strategy: email}  # name suggests an email address
  - notes  # no longer returned by sourceQuery
1 of 61 masked job(s) have drifted. Review the proposals above, then apply them with --apply

It exits 1 when any job has drifted, so it can run in CI beside coverage: coverage catches a new table, and discover --update a new column. --job NAME narrows it to some jobs.

--apply writes the change into each job's file, included ones too: new columns at the end of columns:, marked proposed by discover --update, and stale ones removed, with comments, order and quoting kept. A policy in flow style (columns: {id: keep}) is left as it is, and the error says so. Review what it wrote as you would any policy change.

A job reading one table whole gets proposals from the table, so a new foreign key shares its parent's domain; other queries' columns are classified by name and value. A job with defaultStrategy reports only its stale columns.

docs.title: Your own rules: discovery.yaml
docs.text:
The built-in rules are in bauta/generate/builtinDiscovery.py, and they recognise English column names and US-shaped identifiers. For anything else, such as a national identifier or column names in another language, put rules of your own in configuration/discovery.yaml (or name a file with --rules FILE):

names:                                  # words in column names
- words: [nif, numero_contribuinte]
  policy: {strategy: key, charset: digits}
  reason: a Portuguese tax number
- words: [nome, apelido]
  policy: fakeName
- words: [office_phone]
  policy: keep                          # a switchboard, not a person
  reason: switchboard numbers
values:                                 # regular expressions sampled values must match
- pattern: '[125689]\d{8}'
  policy: {strategy: key, charset: digits}
  reason: looks like a NIF
personalTables: [clientes, utentes]     # a bare `name` column in these is a person's
exclude: [ip]                           # built-in rules to leave out
  • Yours come first, in the order written, and the first match wins, so a rule of yours overrides a built-in one: above, office_phone is kept while home_phone is still masked.
  • names match when any of words is in the column name, split on underscores and camelCase and also run together, so numero_contribuinte matches NumeroContribuinte. A rule is skipped for a column whose type its policy doesn't fit.
  • values match when 80% of a column's sampled values match pattern in full. Unlike the built-in value rules, yours also read integer columns as their digits.
  • policy is a column policy as in jobs.yaml: a strategy name, or a mapping with its options. reason is the comment written beside the proposal; without one, it says the rule came from discovery.yaml.
  • Leaving built-in rules out. exclude drops built-in rules by name, both forms of each; builtins: false drops them all.
Field Required or default Meaning names optional Rules on column names, each with words, a policy and an optional reason. values optional Rules on sampled values, each with a pattern, a policy and an optional reason. personalTables optional Words in a table's name that make a bare name column in it a person's. exclude optional Built-in rules to leave out, by the names below. builtins optional, true false leaves out every built-in rule. Built-in rule Recognises email email addresses, by name and value credential passwords, secrets, tokens and API keys nationalId SSNs, tax ids, passports and licence numbers, by name; 123-45-6789 by value card card numbers, by name, and by value with a Luhn check cardSecurityCode CVV, CVC and CSC codes, by name, proposed as null: PCI DSS forbids storing them bankAccount IBANs, account, routing and sort codes phone phone, mobile and fax numbers, by name and value firstName, lastName, fullName people's names userName user names and logins company companies and employers ip IP addresses, by name, and IPv4 and IPv6 by value, proposed as ip, which keeps each an address; a column named for one whose values aren't all addresses gets hash mac MAC addresses, by name and by value (08:00:2b:01:02:03, 08-00-…, 0800.2b01.0203), proposed as key with charset: hex: a device identifier, kept valid and one-to-one streetAddress, city, postalCode addresses birthDate dates of birth compensation salaries, income and bonuses coordinate latitudes and longitudes, proposed as coordinate, moved up to a kilometre wherever they are; a longitude takes the table's latitude as latitudeColumn where there is exactly one sensitiveAttribute gender, race, ethnicity, religion and nationality, proposed as null: special categories of personal data under GDPR, which shuffle would leave every real value of in the table freeText notes, comments and descriptions uuid UUIDs, by value, proposed as key with charset: hex: other systems (logs, a CRM) may hold the same ids, and key keeps them unique date ISO dates, by value, proposed as keep for review

The same rules, yours included, decide which unmasked columns audit questions and which columns synthesize fills with realistic values. bauta validate checks the file: every pattern must compile, every policy must be valid, and every name in exclude must be a built-in rule.

docs.title: Prove the copy is safe
docs.text: What Where Every column of every job is covered, and references still match once masked bauta audit --connect --strict Every table in production is copied, declared, or fails the build bauta coverage Nothing can ever reach this database unmasked requireMasking on the alias This job copies as it stands, and somebody decided so unmasked: true on the job This table is deliberately not copied, and why acknowledged in jobs.yaml What was masked, how, and under which key, sealed bauta verify-manifest No row in the copy points at a row that isn't there bauta verify-references

docs.title: Reviewing policies: audit
docs.text:
bauta audit                      # offline, from the configuration alone
bauta audit --connect --strict   # also asks the databases; fails on warnings

audit lists every job, whether it masks, and what each masked column gets. It then reports what a reviewer should question — things validation allows, because they can be right:

Severity Finding error A masked query returns a column the policy doesn't cover, or names one it doesn't return (--connect). error A masked query couldn't be run to check (--connect). error A masked job's target table couldn't be read, most often because it doesn't exist yet: create it with schema, or name targetColumns (--connect). error A swap job replaces a table a foreign key in the target references, so the next run can't empty the stage (--connect). warning A swap job replaces a table that declares foreign keys, which the copy stops enforcing every other run (--connect). warning A column is kept unmasked although its name suggests personal data (email, ssn, phone, ...), by the built-in rules or your own. warning A column is kept unmasked although its sampled values look like personal data, whatever it is called (SELECT ssn AS ref with ref: keep), by discover's value rules (--connect). In an unmasked job it is an error. warning A domain whose columns hold values differently (an id as a number and as text, or padded and not), so their masks and references stop matching; normalize makes them agree (--connect). warning defaultStrategy is keep, so any column added to the source later is copied unmasked. warning A job copies from a database without masking while other jobs mask what they read from it. warning A masked job reads over a connection that isn't encrypted, as the server reports it (--connect). warning shuffle on an incremental job, whose small chunks leave values near their own rows. warning An incremental job that run --full-refresh can't replace (no targetTableStage, or a files target), so rows deleted from its source stay in the copy, and a scheduled refresh refuses to run. warning A domain is masked two ways, or under two keys, in one target database, so its masks won't match across the columns that share it. Copies in different target databases may use different keys. warning A foreign-key column isn't masked exactly like the key it references (strategy, options, domain and key), so the copied references won't match (--connect). warning A foreign key and the key it references are both masked with shuffle, which moves values between rows, so the references point at other rows (--connect). warning A job copies only part of a referenced table (a watermark, WHERE, LIMIT or join), and the referencing job isn't limited to match, so the copy can reference rows it lacks (--connect). warning A job's table references another job's, and it can load first: it doesn't wait through predecessors, the other is inactive, or a longer refresh sits between them (--connect). warning A database declares foreign keys only in schemas its jobs don't use, so no reference was checked: set currentSchema, or qualify the jobs' tables (--connect). note Columns that fall to defaultStrategy, by name (--connect). note A target doesn't declare foreign keys its sources do between the tables copied into it, so nothing there stops a row that references nothing; verify-references counts them (--connect). note redact, or json redacting what its fields don't name, which removes identifiers with a recognisable shape but not names. note A column kept unmasked whose sampled values are UUIDs, which other systems may hold too (--connect).

Without --connect, columns are shown as declared. With it, each job's query is run to list the columns it really returns, and its first --sample rows (1,000 by default, 0 for none) are read to question kept columns and shared domains by their values. No value appears in the report, its JSON or its errors.

The foreign-key checks read the keys of each target and of the sources copied into it, as verify-references does, and match them to jobs by table name. A pair of jobs counts as matched for a partial copy when either query names the other's table, as subset's queries and tables that reference each other do. Whether a job waits for another is decided as a run decides it (refresh and predecessors). The swap checks read only the target's own keys, and a job whose postTargetAdhocQueries name the referencing table is taken to recreate them.

audit exits 1 on an error, and with --strict on a warning too, so it can gate CI. Gate it with --connect: offline, select email as contact with contact: keep passes on its name, where the sampled values give it away. --format json writes the report for other tools, --format html one page for a reviewer, and --output FILE to a file; --job narrows it.

docs.title: coverage: what the jobs do not cover
docs.text:
audit checks the jobs that exist, so it can't see a table nobody wrote a job for, which is exactly what a new release adds to production. coverage starts from the database instead, listing every table and what the jobs do with it:

bauta coverage
bauta coverage --connection prod --schema sales
bauta coverage --format json

prod: 4 table(s)

  audit_log                                NOT COVERED
    actor_email                            looks like personal data
  employees                                NOT COVERED
    salary                                 looks like personal data
  countries                                copied as it stands by copyCountries
  customers                                copied and masked by maskCustomers

Covered: 1 masked, 1 copied as they stand, 0 declared not copied. NOT COVERED: 2.
Add a job for each table above, or declare it in `acknowledged` with the reason it is not copied.
State Meaning copied and masked A job reads the table and masks what it reads. copied as it stands A job reads the table with no masking policy. audit reports these too. not copied, declared No job reads it, and acknowledged records why. NOT COVERED No job reads it, and nothing says that was intended.

A table counts as covered when a job reads rows from it: names it after FROM or JOIN, directly or through a CTE, derived table or UNION. A table named only in a comment, a string or a filtering subquery is not covered. A query reaching a table through a view covers it in fact but not here, so declare it.

For a table nothing covers, coverage reads its column names and marks the ones that look like personal data, by the same rules as discover, including your own from discovery.yaml. Columns of covered tables aren't read.

coverage exits 1 when any table is NOT COVERED, so it can follow run in CI and fail the build when production grows a table the copy doesn't account for. --connection picks the alias when the jobs read from more than one; --job narrows which jobs count as covering.

docs.title: A report for reviewers
docs.text:
A privacy or compliance reviewer who doesn't run the CLI can be handed either report as one HTML page:

bauta audit --connect --format html --output audit.html
bauta coverage --format html --output coverage.html

Each opens with a summary, then a section per job (how it masks each column, its key's fingerprint, its findings) or per coverage state.

  • It holds what the text report holds: names, strategies, fingerprints and findings, never a value or a key.
  • One self-contained file, fetching nothing, so it reads the same attached to a ticket or archived beside a release.
  • The exit status is the command's, so the step that writes it can also fail the build.

docs.title: Rotate the masking key
docs.text:
The masking key is a credential, so a security policy usually says to change it on a schedule. A new key changes every mask, so what to do depends on how each copy is loaded.

run refuses to start when an upsert or append job's key changed since it last completed, since its target still holds rows masked under the old key. A swap or overwrite job replaces its whole target, so it needs nothing here.

The job's policy What to do Does not mask the target's primary key bauta run --accept-key-change. Each row is matched on its unchanged key and rewritten under the new one. Masks the target's primary key bauta clear, then bauta run --force. Is incremental, with a targetTableStage bauta run --full-refresh, either way: the target is replaced whole under the new key, with no moment when it's empty. Appends to files or an Iceberg table Remove what the job wrote (bauta clear empties only database tables), then bauta run --accept-key-change --force. Acknowledging the change without removing the old rows leaves a table half of which won't join to the other half.

run refuses the second case whatever flags are given. An upsert matches on the primary key, and a new masking key gives every masked key a new value, so the run would insert a second generation of rows beside the first, sometimes over other rows' data, leaving a target whose foreign keys all still resolve, so that verify-references passes it.

bauta clear empties the targets children-first and forgets the recorded key, so the next run starts afresh:

export MASKING_KEY=<the new key>
bauta clear --yes           # empties the jobs' targets, children first
bauta run --force           # reloads everything under the new key

--force stops a job inside its refresh window leaving its emptied target empty. Run the jobs together, so columns sharing a domain reload under one key and still join.

The masking key is not BAUTA_MANIFEST_KEY, which signs manifests, so older manifests stay verifiable, each recording the key fingerprint it was made under.

docs.title: Run from Airflow or Dagster
docs.text:
bauta run makes one pass and exits, so an orchestrator runs it like any command, its exit code the task's outcome. example/orchestrators/ has working files for both, and a demo that needs neither.

File What it is bautaTasks.py What both build from: the job graph, and the command each task runs. Copy it beside your DAG or Dagster code. airflowDag.py One task a run, every 15 minutes, and a weekly full refresh after the checks. airflowDagPerJob.py A task per bauta job, downstream of its predecessors. dagsterDefinitions.py An asset per bauta job, with an incremental and a full-refresh job over them. demo.py Runs a task per job the way both do, with no orchestrator: python example/orchestrators/demo.py.

docs.title: Run the command, not the Python API
docs.text:
Each task runs bauta in a process of its own: runDataJobs starts each job in a new process, which re-imports the calling program, and in a worker that is the orchestrator itself. The command's exit codes also map onto a task's outcome:

Exit code The task 0 succeeded: every job completed 1 failed: a job failed or was skipped, or another run holds the jobs 2 failed: the configuration or the command is wrong, so retrying won't help 130 was stopped

--quiet leaves only errors in the task's log, one line each; add --log FILE --log-format json for the full record. bautaTasks.command() runs python -m bauta with the worker's interpreter, or whatever $BAUTA_COMMAND says (a virtualenv's bauta, docker run … bauta).

The scheduler parses DAG files often, usually without your secrets, so jobGraph() reads the jobs file and its includes as written, expanding and validating nothing; a bauta validate task checks the configuration when it runs.

docs.title: One task a run, or a task per job
docs.text:
One task a run (airflowDag.py) is simplest: bauta decides what runs, in what order and how many at once, by workers, refresh, predecessors and maxConcurrentJobs, as under cron. The orchestrator sees one task.

A task per job (airflowDagPerJob.py, dagsterDefinitions.py) gives each job its own log, duration, retry and place in the graph, and Dagster's lineage shows what each copy is built from. The orchestrator then decides what bauta did:

  • How many at once: each task runs one job, so workers and maxConcurrentJobs limit nothing. An Airflow pool or Dagster concurrency key stands in for workers; give a connection that needs a limit a pool of its own.
  • When: --job ignores refresh, so every task runs whenever the DAG does. Schedule it as often as the most frequent job needs, or split cadences into DAGs of their own.
  • After a failure: the orchestrator skips a failed job's dependents, as bauta does.

run --job holds only its own jobs' locks, so tasks for different jobs run side by side, and the same job never twice at once.

docs.title: The weekly refresh and the checks
docs.text:
Both examples schedule run --full-refresh weekly, taking deleted rows out of incremental copies. In Airflow it follows two checks, so a policy fallen behind production fails a check rather than the refresh:

  1. bauta audit --strict: among other things, any incremental job a full refresh can't replace.
  2. bauta discover --update: any column production has gained or lost that a policy doesn't match (keeping a policy up to date).

A refresh and a regular run can reach the same job at once. With one task a run, give both DAGs' run tasks one slot of one pool; with a task per job, the second to start a job exits 1, so give tasks a retry after a pause.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text: bauta reads the masking key and passwords from its environment. In Airflow, airflowDag.py renders MASKING_KEY from a Variable, which a secrets backend keeps out of Airflow's database; in Dagster, set it in the code location's environment. passwordCommand fetches short-lived database credentials either way.

docs.title: Run on a schedule
docs.text: Running bauta unattended: where its state lives, and what to do after a failure. For why it runs once and exits, see how it works.

docs.title: A deployment, put together
docs.text:
In /etc/etl/jobs.yaml, beside the jobs:

memory: /var/lib/etl/memory.yaml
history:
  connection: warehouse
manifest:
  connection: warehouse

*/15 * * * *  bauta run --config /etc/etl --log-format json --log /var/log/etl/etl.log --quiet
0 3 * * 0     bauta run --config /etc/etl --full-refresh --log-format json --log /var/log/etl/etl.log --quiet

The second line is a weekly full refresh, so rows deleted in production leave the copy within a week; a 15-minute run starting during it exits with status 1 rather than overlap. With BAUTA_NOTIFY_URL set, a failed run posts to the team's channel; bauta history says what happened overnight, and bauta verify-manifest checks the latest manifest.

docs.title: Run state
docs.text:
run keeps each job's last run time, watermark and key fingerprint between invocations. Losing it breaks nothing, but every incremental job re-extracts from watermarkInitial and refresh windows start over.

Where Set with Use when A file named by jobs.yaml's memory, relative to it; memory.yaml beside it without one (default) The filesystem persists between runs. A table memory: {connection: ALIAS} in jobs.yaml Nothing persists: containers without a volume, several machines. Another file, or a table, for one run --memory FILE, --memory-connection ALIAS It should live somewhere else this time, such as a mounted volume.

In a table, a watermark is stored as text with its type, and read back as that type, bytes such as SQL Server's rowversion included. See tables for the definition.

Overlapping runs. run holds a lock beside the memory file (memory.yaml.run.lock) while it runs, and a second run finding it held exits with status 1. A run --job locks only its own jobs, so runs of different jobs go side by side, as an orchestrator's task per job does, while the same job never runs twice at once. With run state in a table, the lock is a local file, so it only separates runs on one machine; across machines, let the scheduler do it (a CronJob's concurrencyPolicy: Forbid, Airflow's max_active_runs=1).

docs.title: After a failed cycle
docs.text:
A failed job's dependents are skipped, so nothing loads rows whose parents are missing, and each skip is recorded with its cause.

Cycle finished: 14 completed, 1 failed, 1 skipped, 1374 row(s) moved

refresh is the resume mechanism, so a plain bauta run is the right next step: completed jobs are inside their window and skipped, while the failed one runs again and its dependents follow.

What you want Command Retry what failed, leave the rest bauta run Re-run everything, ignoring refresh bauta run --force Re-run one job and nothing else bauta run --job NAME (its predecessors don't run; run warns about each)

Without refresh, a plain run reruns every job: correct, but more work than needed.

docs.title: One production, several environments
docs.text:
One jobs.yaml can fill dev, staging and UAT from one production, two ways that combine.

A connections file per environment, named by --connections, so the jobs never change:

bauta run --connections environments/staging.yaml
bauta run --connections environments/uat.yaml

An alias from the environment: ${NAME} expands anywhere in jobs.yaml, targetConnection included, and the alias is checked offline:

defaults:
  sourceConnection: prod
  targetConnection: ${TARGET_ALIAS:-staging}

$ TARGET_ALIAS=nosuchalias bauta validate
Invalid job graph:
maskCountries: targetConnection "nosuchalias" is not a known connection alias

Give each environment its own masking key, so their copies can't be joined to each other's, unless a tester needs to follow a record across them. Either way, requireMasking on each target says none can ever receive unmasked rows.

docs.title: Studio
docs.text:
Preview

Studio is new. Its screens, settings and stored data may change between releases without a deprecation period, and it has been tested on SQLite more than on server databases. It runs as one process, and sees live runs only on its own machine. The CLI is unaffected either way.

bauta Studio is a web console for a team, run on your own infrastructure. People sign in to watch runs, start and rerun them, prove the copy is safe, and change jobs, without a shell on the machine holding production's credentials. Everything it shows, the bauta command can too.

Studio reads the configuration, run state, history and manifests run keeps, and starts runs as the same bauta run cron does, so your schedule stays where it is.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
pip install "bauta[studio]"
bauta studio create-user --config /etc/bauta/configuration --email you@example.com
bauta studio serve --config /etc/bauta/configuration

create-user makes an admin (unless --role says otherwise), asking for a password of 12 characters or more, or none with --sso-only. It is the only way to make the first account, since an open sign-up page would be a hole. People change their own password on their Account page; an admin sets a forgotten one on the Users page, as Studio sends no email.

Locked out, say with the only admin's password forgotten or their authenticator lost with its recovery codes? Reset it from the server's shell, which signs the account out everywhere; --reset-2fa also turns two-factor sign-in off, to set up again:

bauta studio set-password --config /etc/bauta/configuration --email you@example.com --reset-2fa

serve listens on 127.0.0.1:8710, this machine only. To share it, put it behind a proxy that terminates TLS (nginx, Caddy, a cloud load balancer), with --host 0.0.0.0 and --forwarded-allow-ips naming the proxy if it is on another machine. Run one process: it keeps track of the runs it starts.

Give Studio your cron job's environment: the variables the configuration names (${MASKING_KEY}, passwords) must be set, and BAUTA_MANIFEST_KEY lets it verify signed manifests.

Setting Default --config, $BAUTA_STUDIO_CONFIG $BAUTA_CONFIG, else ./configuration bauta's jobs.yaml and connections.yaml. --data, $BAUTA_STUDIO_DATA ./studio-data Studio's own: accounts, the activity log, run logs, and the jobs files as they were before each edit. Keep it on a persistent volume. $BAUTA_STUDIO_DATABASE_URL SQLite in the data directory Any SQLAlchemy URL, PostgreSQL say, for Studio's tables. $BAUTA_STUDIO_INSECURE_COOKIES=1 off Only for plain HTTP on your own machine. $BAUTA_STUDIO_TRANSFORM_MODULES none Comma-separated modules an edit may start naming in a transform or custom masking strategy. See what it protects. $BAUTA_STUDIO_PASSWORD_LOGIN all Who may sign in with a password: all, admins or off. Anything but all needs single sign-on. $BAUTA_STUDIO_SESSION_HOURS 12 How long a password session lasts. $BAUTA_STUDIO_REQUIRE_2FA off, or admins with single sign-on Whose password also needs an authenticator code; see two-factor sign-in. $BAUTA_STUDIO_SECRET_KEY_FILE secret.key in the data directory The key two-factor secrets are encrypted with.

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.text:
Studio signs people in through your identity provider with OpenID Connect: Okta, Entra ID, Google Workspace, Auth0, Keycloak, or any provider with a discovery document.

  1. At the provider, register a web application (a confidential client) with the redirect URI https://<studio's address>/api/auth/sso/callback, and note its issuer, client ID and client secret.

  2. Give Studio these, and restart it:

    BAUTA_STUDIO_PUBLIC_URL=https://studio.example.com
BAUTA_STUDIO_OIDC_ISSUER=https://example.okta.com
BAUTA_STUDIO_OIDC_CLIENT_ID=0oa...
BAUTA_STUDIO_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET_FILE=/run/secrets/studio-oidc

  3. Add people on the Users page with no password, or let them make their own accounts. The sign-in page then offers the provider.

Then make the provider the way in:

  • BAUTA_STUDIO_PASSWORD_LOGIN=admins, leaving passwords only to break-glass admins, the way in if the provider is down or misconfigured. Make one with create-user under an email the provider doesn't have, such as break-glass@example.com; serve warns when no active admin has a password. Under all, someone linked keeps their password, so disabling them at the provider doesn't keep them out: remove it on the Users page.
  • Two-factor sign-in for those passwords, on for admins by default once single sign-on is.
Setting Default $BAUTA_STUDIO_PUBLIC_URL required Where browsers reach Studio, with no path. The redirect URI is built from it, never from the request. $BAUTA_STUDIO_OIDC_ISSUER off The provider's issuer, exactly as its discovery document names it, trailing slash and all. Setting it turns single sign-on on. $BAUTA_STUDIO_OIDC_CLIENT_ID required $BAUTA_STUDIO_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET, ..._CLIENT_SECRET_FILE none The secret, or a file holding it. Sent with HTTP Basic unless the provider takes it only in the request body. $BAUTA_STUDIO_OIDC_LABEL Sign in with SSO The sign-in button's words, such as Sign in with Okta. $BAUTA_STUDIO_OIDC_SCOPES openid email profile Space-separated. Add groups, or your provider's name for it, if groups set roles. $BAUTA_STUDIO_OIDC_SESSION_HOURS 8 How long a session through the provider lasts; someone disabled there keeps theirs until it ends. $BAUTA_STUDIO_OIDC_TRUST_EMAIL=1 off Link by email even when the provider doesn't vouch for it. See who gets an account. $BAUTA_STUDIO_OIDC_AUTO_CREATE=1 off Make an account at a person's first sign-in. Needs ..._ALLOWED_DOMAINS. $BAUTA_STUDIO_OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS none Comma-separated email domains whose people get an account at first sign-in. A subdomain is another domain. $BAUTA_STUDIO_OIDC_HOSTED_DOMAINS none For Google Workspace: the workspaces whose accounts may sign in, by the token's hd claim. $BAUTA_STUDIO_OIDC_ROLES studio studio: admins set roles on the Users page. provider: groups at the provider set them. $BAUTA_STUDIO_OIDC_ROLE_CLAIM groups The claim listing a person's groups; a dotted name reaches inside an object, such as realm_access.roles. $BAUTA_STUDIO_OIDC_ADMIN_GROUPS, ..._OPERATOR_GROUPS, ..._VIEWER_GROUPS none For ROLES=provider: comma-separated groups giving each role, as the claim names them. Someone in several gets the highest.

Studio refuses to start with a setting missing or wrong, naming it. serve reads the provider's discovery document as it starts and warns if it can't, then starts anyway and says so at sign-in. Its log says why any sign-in was refused.

docs.title: Who gets an account
docs.text:
Once linked, a person is matched by the provider's issuer and subject, which the provider gives no one else. The subject is kept as its SHA-256, so two differing only in case stay two people on databases that ignore case.

The first time, a person is linked by email, but only if the provider vouches for it (email_verified, or Entra ID's xms_edov): a provider that let people set their own email would otherwise let anyone take over an account. Set TRUST_EMAIL=1 only for a provider whose emails only its admins set.

  • Made at first sign-in: under AUTO_CREATE, someone with no account gets one if their email is in an allowed domain, as a viewer or with the role their groups give. Otherwise they are told to ask an admin.
  • Passwords: linking removes a password the policy wouldn't let the account use. A break-glass admin under PASSWORD_LOGIN=admins is never linked; its sign-in through the provider is refused.
  • Emails: an email changed at the provider follows to Studio if the provider vouches for it and no other account has it.
  • Linked twice: an account linked to one identity refuses another from the same issuer. When a person's identity there was remade, an admin unlinks the account on the Users page and the next sign-in links it anew. One linked under another issuer is relinked by itself.
  • Deactivated accounts are refused through the provider too.

docs.title: Roles from the provider
docs.text:
With BAUTA_STUDIO_OIDC_ROLES=provider, a person's role is set from their groups at each sign-in, and the Users page shows it but can't change it. Someone with no group giving a role is refused, with no account made. A change takes effect at the next sign-in, so a session keeps its role until it ends. Accounts not linked to the provider, the break-glass admin among them, keep the roles set in Studio. The provider can't demote the last active admin: that sign-in is refused, saying why.

Groups are read from the ID token, or from the userinfo endpoint when the token leaves them out.

docs.title: Signing out, and logs
docs.text:
Signing out ends Studio's session, not the provider's, so the next sign-in through it won't ask for a password while the provider's session lasts.

The callback's address holds a one-time authorization code, which Studio keeps out of its access log. A proxy in front logs it too; it is useless without what only the browser that began the sign-in held, but you may want the proxy to leave out the query for /api/auth/sso/callback.

docs.title: Notes by provider
docs.text:
• Okta: the issuer is your org's (https://example.okta.com) or an authorization server's (.../oauth2/default). For roles, add a groups claim to the ID token, filtered to Studio's groups, and add groups to SCOPES for the org authorization server.
  • Entra ID: the issuer is https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant id>/v2.0. Entra sends no email_verified, so add the xms_edov optional claim, which Studio accepts instead. TRUST_EMAIL=1 is safe only in a tenant with no guest users. For roles, define app roles and set ROLE_CLAIM=roles: a groups claim names groups by object ID and is cut off past 200.
  • Google Workspace: the issuer is https://accounts.google.com. Set HOSTED_DOMAINS to your workspace, or a personal Google account made with a work email, whose email is also verified, could sign in. Google has no groups claim, so set roles in Studio.
  • Keycloak: the issuer is https://<host>/realms/<realm>. For roles, add a group membership mapper with full group path off, or read realm roles with ROLE_CLAIM=realm_access.roles after turning on "Add to ID token" for the realm roles mapper.

docs.title: Two-factor sign-in
docs.text:
A password can also ask for a code from an authenticator app (1Password, Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, any that does TOTP). Signing in through the identity provider never does: the provider asks for its own second factor.

Anyone with a password sets it up on their Account page: scan a QR code, type the code the app shows, and keep the ten one-time recovery codes for a lost app. BAUTA_STUDIO_REQUIRE_2FA makes it required:

$BAUTA_STUDIO_REQUIRE_2FA off Anyone may set it up. The default without single sign-on. admins Admins set it up at their next sign-in, before they are signed in, and can't turn it off. The default with single sign-on, when an admin's password is the break-glass way in. all Everyone with a password.

An admin resets it on the Users page for someone who lost both app and recovery codes.

  • Codes are taken once each; one a step either side of now is accepted too, for a drifting phone clock. Ten wrong codes for an account in five minutes, five from one address, or thirty from one address across accounts, and more are refused for a while.
  • Secrets are encrypted with a key Studio makes in its data directory, secret.key, readable by its account alone, so the database or a backup of it can't make codes without the key. Keep the key apart with $BAUTA_STUDIO_SECRET_KEY_FILE, and back it up: lose it, and everyone's two-factor sign-in must be reset.
  • Recovery codes are kept only as their SHA-256, and each signs in once.

docs.title: Who can do what
docs.text: Role Can viewer read every screen operator also start, rerun and cancel runs, and run the checks that connect to the databases: dry runs, a connected audit, coverage, discovery, connection tests admin also edit the jobs files, manage users, and read the activity log

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• Overview: the last run, failing and stale jobs, what the latest checks found new (a table no job covers, a column no policy names, a broken reference), the audit's findings, whether the last manifest verifies, and where recent runs spent their time.
  • Runs: every run, from the schedule or from Studio. A running one updates as it goes, each job waiting, running with its rows so far, or done; see what's running now.
  • Cancelling a run stops it as Ctrl-C would: jobs not started are skipped and loading ones finish, so no target is left half loaded. A run on another machine is cancelled there.
  • Start a run offers a full refresh only when every incremental job can take one, and says why not when one can't.
  • Jobs: each job's policy by strategy and key fingerprint, how it loads, its trend of rows and duration, its recent runs, and its speed against the source, measured as bauta bench measures it.
  • Comparing runs: two runs job by job: status, rows, duration, the stage that slowed it and, where both manifests are kept, the columns masked differently.
  • Schedule: each job's place (due, inside its refresh window, inactive), when it last ran, and whether it is stale.
  • Proof: coverage of every source, each copy's references as verify-references counts them, the audit, every manifest and whether it verifies, and an evidence bundle per run for a reviewer (what ran, its manifest and verification, the audit and coverage, whether the jobs files are still those it used, and a SHA-256 of every file). Studio keeps each manifest by run as it appears; cron runs in quick succession can replace one before Studio sees it, so to be sure of every run's, keep manifests in a table.
  • Discovery: columns a source gained since its policy was written, with the policy discover proposes, to accept into the jobs file.
  • Subset builder: a subset from a root table and a filter, previewed in load order with row counts, which tables the target lacks and which another job already loads, then added to a jobs file. The filter is SQL run against the source as written, so only an admin builds one.
  • Connections: each alias, where it points and its rules, with a connection test. Never a password.
  • Configuration: the jobs files, edited in place as text or job by job in a form.

docs.title: Nightly checks
docs.text: Coverage, the connected audit, discovery and references read the sources, so they run when an operator asks, or daily at a time an admin sets on the Proof page (in UTC); a Studio that was down then runs them as it starts. Each result is kept with who ran it, and what a check finds new is listed on the Overview, so a table or column production gained last night reaches someone before a job copies it.

docs.title: What it protects
docs.text:
• Single sign-on: the authorization code flow with PKCE. The state tying a sign-in to its browser is in a signed cookie sent only to the callback, lasting ten minutes. The ID token must be signed by a key the provider publishes, asymmetrically, for this client, by this issuer, unexpired, with this sign-in's nonce. The provider's keys are re-read within the hour, so a withdrawn key stops being trusted. Each sign-in is taken once, failed ones are counted by address, only HTTPS reaches the provider and Studio (but for local addresses), and a new sign-in ends the browser's old session.
  • Accounts: argon2 password hashes. Five failed sign-ins for an email from one address in five minutes, thirty from one address across emails, or a hundred for one email across addresses, and more are refused for a while, so failing from one address doesn't lock the owner out from another (give --forwarded-allow-ips your proxy, or every sign-in counts as its address). At most four passwords are checked at once. Sessions are random tokens kept only as their SHA-256, in an HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, Secure cookie. Changing a password or deactivating a user signs them out everywhere, and the last admin can't be removed.
  • Requests from other sites: every change needs the X-Bauta-Studio header, which another site can't send without a CORS preflight Studio never answers. Pages carry a strict Content-Security-Policy and can't be framed.
  • What leaves the server: what bauta audit and bauta history show: names, strategies, key fingerprints, counts, times and scrubbed errors. Never a masking key, a password, connections.yaml, or a table's value.
  • Editing: only jobs.yaml and the files it includes. A change is written, atomically, only if the whole configuration still validates with it and the file is unchanged since it was opened; the old file is kept, and the change recorded with its diff and author.
  • Admins are trusted with the server. Editing a job changes what SQL runs against your databases, as Studio's account. An edit can't start naming a transform or custom strategy from a module the jobs files don't already use (beyond bauta's own and $BAUTA_STUDIO_TRANSFORM_MODULES), since os:system is a callable too, and the edit is refused before anything is imported; DuckDB queries can't reach the machine's files (DuckDB). That closes the shortest path from an edit to a command, not every path: give the role accordingly.
  • Its own files: the data directory, run logs and backups are created readable by Studio's account alone. An existing directory keeps its permissions; chmod 700 it.
  • Upgrades: Studio migrates its own tables as it starts, keeping what they hold. Back up its database first, as you would any other.
  • Runs: each a bauta run process in a session of its own, under bauta's lock, so a run from Studio and one from cron never overlap on the same jobs, and restarting Studio doesn't stop one.

docs.title: Run history
docs.text:
With history set in jobs.yaml, run records one entry per job after each cycle: a JSON line in a file, or a row in a table. Nothing reads it to decide what to run; it's for answering "what happened last night".

history: ../transaction/history.jsonl    # a file, relative to jobs.yaml
history:
  connection: warehouse                  # or a table

bauta history
bauta history --job loadOrders --limit 5
bauta history --format json

FINISHED (UTC)       JOB                          STATUS           ROWS   SECONDS    READ    MASK   WRITE  WAITED  ERROR
2026-09-16 02:00:14  loadInvoices                 skipped             0       0.0       -       -       -       -  predecessor(s) did not complete: loadCustomers
2026-09-16 02:00:13  loadCustomers                failed              0       1.0       -       -       -       -  OperationalError: timeout
2026-09-16 02:00:12  loadOrders                   completed        4200      12.5     2.1     1.4    10.3     0.0

--history FILE or --history-connection ALIAS overrides the setting, on run and on history.

Each record has runId (shared by the jobs of one cycle), job, status, rowCount, attempts, startedAt, finishedAt, durationSeconds and error, cut to 2000 characters, and for a job that completed, readSeconds, maskSeconds, writeSeconds and throttledSeconds (see where the time went). A file grows by one line per job per run, so rotate it with logrotate or similar.

docs.title: Where the time went
docs.text:
READ, MASK and WRITE are the seconds a completed job spent busy at each stage:

  • read: running the query and fetching rows from the source, and nothing else.
  • mask: transforming and masking them.
  • write: loading them into the target, and whatever it takes to finish: a swap, an upsert from the stage table, a file published or an Iceberg commit.
  • waited (throttledSeconds): held back by the source's read limit.

They are busy time: with the native masker the stages overlap, so they add up to more than SECONDS, and the largest sets the job's pace. In the example loadOrders waited on its target, so a faster masker would change nothing. Partitions add theirs together. A history table from 0.2.4 or earlier records them once it has their columns. The same four appear as stages in JSON logs and notifications, and bauta bench measures them without writing.

Alerting on staleness. History in a table answers the question worth alerting on, whether a job has stopped completing, from any monitor that runs SQL. Alert on that rather than one failure, which a retry may already have fixed:

SELECT job, max(finished_at) AS last_success
FROM bauta_history
WHERE status = 'completed'
GROUP BY job
HAVING max(finished_at) < <now, in seconds since 1970> - 3 * 3600

docs.title: What's running now
docs.text:
bauta status shows each run in progress and where each of its jobs stands: waiting for a predecessor or a free worker, running since when, or completed, failed or skipped, with its rows or its error.

bauta status
bauta status --format json

Run 0b6c1f0e-4d1e-4f7a-9a43-2f0c9f6a1d52, started 2026-10-16 02:00:03 UTC: running, process 48121
  1 completed, 1 running, 1 waiting
  JOB                          STATUS     STARTED (UTC)              ROWS  ERROR
  loadCustomers                completed  2026-10-16 02:00:03       12000
  loadOrders                   running    2026-10-16 02:00:41           -
  loadInvoices                 waiting    -                             -

While a cycle runs, run keeps a small JSON file for it beside its run-state lock (in memory.yaml.running/), rewritten as each job starts or is decided and removed when the cycle ends. It holds what the table shows, never a value from a table. A file left by a run whose process is gone is shown as ended without finishing. With run state in a table, status sees runs started on its own machine.

A cycle's run id is the same here, in history and in a manifest table. From Python, Project.running() reads the same files, and runDataJobs(onProgress=...) is told each change (the library).

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
--notify-url URL, or $BAUTA_NOTIFY_URL, posts JSON to a webhook when a cycle doesn't succeed: a job failed or was skipped, or a signal stopped the run. --notify-on always posts after every cycle.

{
  "text": "bauta on etl-7d9f: failed -- 1 completed, 1 failed, 1 skipped, 4200 row(s)\n- loadCustomers failed: OperationalError: timeout\n- loadInvoices skipped: predecessor(s) did not complete: loadCustomers",
  "status": "failed",
  "host": "etl-7d9f",
  "summary": {"completed": 1, "failed": 1, "skipped": 1, "rows": 4200},
  "jobs": [{"job": "loadOrders", "status": "completed", "rowCount": 4200, "durationSeconds": 12.5, "error": null,
            "readSeconds": 2.1, "maskSeconds": 1.4, "writeSeconds": 10.3, "throttledSeconds": 0.0}, "..."]
}

Slack, Mattermost and Teams incoming webhooks show text as it is; anything else can read the rest. A post that fails on the network, times out, or gets a 5xx or 429 is sent once more, three seconds later; any other answer is logged. The URL usually carries a token, so prefer the environment variable. Error text is scrubbed of the values drivers quote in every known format, not every possible one; choose the channel with that in mind.

History and notifications never affect a run's outcome: a failure is logged, and the run carries on.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[all,dev]" ./mask-rs/py    # leave off ./mask-rs/py without Rust
pytest
ruff check
mypy                                         # targets Python 3.10, the oldest supported

docs.title: The default test run
docs.text:
pytest needs no servers. It covers everything that doesn't need a real network database, which is most of the package:

  • Unit tests against mocked cursors, verifying the SQL each dialect builds and the control flow around it.
  • Real SQLite, end to end — tests/integration/test_integration_sqlite.py runs real streaming and incremental loads through real worker processes. It isn't marked integration, since SQLite ships with Python and needs no service.
  • The CLI, driven through main() against a real SQLite database, including its exit codes, and discover and subset output that is then run.
  • Masking end to end through real worker processes (tests/masking/test_masking_end_to_end.py), and the masking strategies' properties (tests/masking/test_masking.py): determinism, consistency within a domain, one-to-one keys, and preserved types.
  • The shipped examples: every configuration/ under example/ is validated against the real models, and every demo is run end to end, so none can drift from what the code accepts.
  • With the native masker installed, Python against Rust over the same values (tests/masking/test_nativeMasking.py), on one thread and on eight, with identical masks and errors required.

A connection or file left open, by the package or by a test, fails the run: ResourceWarning is an error. The garbage collector finds a leak later than it happened, so the failure is charged to whichever test is running then; PYTHONTRACEMALLOC=20 pytest shows where the object was opened.

tests/conftest.py stubs oracledb and psycopg where they aren't installed, so the default run needs no client libraries. It also creates the package's logger before any test and detaches the handlers each test adds, since caplog only reaches a non-propagating logger that exists when the test starts.

docs.title: Where the tests are
docs.text:
tests/ mirrors the package: tests/jobs/ tests bauta/jobs/, and so on; tests/test_project.py covers bauta/project.py. Studio's tests run through its API, and are skipped without the studio extra. Three folders don't follow a package:

  • tests/integration/: against real databases (all but SQLite marked integration).
  • tests/examples/: every demo and the masking benchmark run, and every shipped configuration validated.
  • tests/repository/: the docs' links and the packaging.
