docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Runnable demonstrations, and a starter configuration to copy. None needs a server or credentials; each runs against throwaway SQLite databases. The test suite runs every one, so none can drift from what the code accepts.

Each demo has the same shape:

File or folder What it is demo.py the script: python example/<demo>/demo.py from the repository root configuration/ what it reads: connections.yaml, and jobs.yaml where the demo doesn't generate its own transaction/ what it writes: databases, run state, logs, manifests. Emptied at the start of each run, and ignored by git

The walkthrough runs the bauta command itself. The other demos call the Python API, and before each step print the bauta command that does the same, with the environment variables its configuration/ reads — paste it into a shell from the repository root to run that step yourself.

Demo Shows walkthrough/ the whole workflow, through the commands a person would type incremental/ streaming, and incremental loads that extract only what changed masking/ masking, discovery and subsetting, from Python orchestrators/ bauta under Airflow and Dagster: a DAG, a DAG with a task per job, and Dagster assets, with a demo that runs a task per job without either native-masking/ Python against Rust on a narrow table, and Rust on one core against all of them on a wide one: the speed, and identical results starter/ not a demo: a configuration to copy for your own databases

docs.title: walkthrough
docs.text:
python example/walkthrough/demo.py

Builds a small shop's "production" database -- customers with national ids and phone numbers, orders, support tickets full of personal details, and payment cards -- and makes a safe staging copy of its Portuguese and Spanish customers:

  1. discover proposes a masking policy.
  2. subset --mask generates a job per table for those customers and everything they reference. The script then applies what a reviewer would decide, and records each decision at the top of the jobs file: masked ids sharing domains, fpe for national ids, redact for ticket text, and no copy at all of payment cards.
  3. schema creates staging's tables.
  4. audit --connect --strict checks the reviewed policy against production.
  5. run copies and masks, writing a signed manifest and run history.
  6. verify-manifest checks the manifest.
  7. synthesize fills staging's payment cards with generated rows.
  8. history shows what ran.

Its configuration/ holds only connections.yaml, since subset generates the jobs into transaction/. It ends by showing customers and a support ticket before and after, including what redact leaves behind, and writes the session to transaction/walkthrough.md.

Tested by tests/examples/test_walkthrough.py, which also checks that no production email, phone number or card number reaches staging.

docs.title: incremental
docs.text:
python example/incremental/demo.py

Loads its job the way the CLI does -- YAML, then ${NAME} expansion, then validation -- and runs it three times against one SQLite database.

Watch the second run: between runs, a loaded row is edited without its updatedAt changing, and a new row added. An incremental run sees only the new row, and the unchanged edit is the tell.

Tested by tests/examples/test_incremental_demo.py.

docs.title: masking
docs.text:
python example/masking/demo.py

Builds a "production" and a "staging" SQLite database, then:

  1. Masks customers and orders into staging. The two tables still join, because customers.id and orders.customer_id share the customer domain.
  2. Adds an ssn column to production, which the policy doesn't cover. The next run fails before writing anything, and staging is left as it was. New columns never leak by default.
  3. Proposes a policy for the changed table, as bauta discover does.
  4. Plans a subset of European customers and their orders, as bauta subset does.

It uses a throwaway key unless MASKING_KEY is already set.

Tested by tests/examples/test_masking_demo.py.

docs.title: orchestrators
docs.text:
python example/orchestrators/demo.py

Working Airflow and Dagster files, described in run from Airflow or Dagster, and a demo that runs a bauta run --job process per job, each once its predecessors finish, as both orchestrators do. It deletes an order in production, which an incremental run leaves in the copy, and the weekly checks and full refresh take out.

Tested by tests/examples/test_orchestrators.py, which also loads each orchestrator's file against stand-ins, since Airflow and Dagster are too heavy to install for the suite.

docs.title: native-masking
docs.text:
python example/native-masking/demo.py                  # 100,000 narrow rows and 1,000,000 wide ones: about 2½ minutes
python example/native-masking/demo.py 100000 200000    # the same comparison, quicker

Masks two tables in Python and in Rust (the native masker, bauta-rs), each run into a staging copy of its own, and checks every copy of a table is identical.

A narrow table, six masked columns, where writing to the database sets the pace. Reading, masking and writing take turns or overlap (BAUTA_PIPELINE), in Python or in Rust (BAUTA_NATIVE):

Narrow table: 100,000 rows, 6 masked columns
                                 seconds   rows a second     vs first
Python, in turn                      7.4          13,587         1.0x
Python, overlapped                   7.4          13,511         1.0x
Rust, in turn                        1.5          65,919         4.9x
Rust, overlapped                     1.0          96,077         7.1x

A wide table, 25 masked columns, where masking sets the pace. Rust masks on one core or on the half of them auto takes (BAUTA_MASKING_THREADS):

Wide table: 1,000,000 rows, 25 masked columns
                                 seconds   rows a second     vs first
Rust, in turn                       39.2          25,519         1.0x
Rust, overlapped                    32.6          30,691         1.2x
Rust, in turn, auto threads         15.5          64,612         2.5x
Rust, overlapped, auto threads       9.4         106,080         4.2x

On a ten-core M1 Pro, where auto masks on five. Overlapping gains little for Python, whose masking leaves no wait to hide, and more for Rust; against a remote database it gains more still. The narrow table runs on one core only, since its time goes to writing.

Without the extension, the demo runs the Python runs and says how to install it (pip install ./mask-rs/py, with Rust 1.83 or newer).

Tested by tests/examples/test_native_masking_demo.py.

docs.title: starter
docs.text:
A complete configuration to start your own from:

mkdir configuration
cp example/starter/configuration/*.yaml configuration/
File What it holds connections.yaml two database aliases, with credentials read from the environment jobs.yaml a defaults: block, data jobs including an incremental one and two masked ones, and run state, history and the manifest kept in transaction/

Set the variables it reads -- SOURCE_DB_PASSWORD, TARGET_DB_PASSWORD and MASKING_KEY -- then edit it for your databases. The CLI reads ./configuration by default; --config DIR points it anywhere else.

Validated, with every demo's configuration, by tests/examples/test_shipped_example_configuration.py. See docs/reference/configuration.md for every field.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
What changed in each release of bauta and bauta-rs, which are always released together at the same version. Breaking lists what can stop an existing setup working after an upgrade; read it first.

Masks never change between releases unless an entry says so: the same value, key and domain give the same mask in every version so far.

docs.title: 0.2.12 — 2026-11-22
docs.text: Studio signs people in through your identity provider (OpenID Connect single sign-on, for Okta, Entra ID, Google Workspace, Auth0, Keycloak and the rest), and can ask for a code from an authenticator app after a password. See single sign-on and two-factor sign-in. No mask changes.

docs.title: Breaking
docs.text:
• A Studio database from an earlier release must be made again: its tables were changed in place, not by a migration. Stop Studio, move the database aside (studio.db in the data directory, or the one BAUTA_STUDIO_DATABASE_URL names), start it, and add the accounts again.
  • /api/auth/me's refusal and /api/users say more: how the sign-in page offers to sign in, and how each account signs in.
  • A right password may not sign in yet: /api/auth/login answers {"twoFactorStep": ...} for an account that needs a code next, or must set an app up first.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Single sign-on for Studio, by the authorization code flow with PKCE. The ID token is checked against the provider's published keys, by asymmetric algorithms only. Once linked, a person is matched by the provider's issuer and subject, never by email; before that, only by an email the provider vouches for, so a provider letting people set their own email can't hand over an account.
  • Accounts are made by an admin, or at first sign-in for the email domains you allow.
  • Roles are set on the Users page, or from the person's groups at the provider on every sign-in (BAUTA_STUDIO_OIDC_ROLES=provider).
  • Passwords stay for everyone, for admins only (a break-glass account for when the provider is down), or are turned off (BAUTA_STUDIO_PASSWORD_LOGIN). Linking removes a password the policy wouldn't allow; a break-glass admin is never linked; the provider's groups can't demote the last admin.
  • Sessions through the provider last 8 hours by default, against a password's 12, so someone disabled there loses access sooner.
  • Admins can add an account with no password, and unlink one whose identity at the provider was remade. bauta studio create-user --sso-only does the same.
  • The callback's authorization code is kept out of the access log.
  • Google Workspace sign-ins can be limited to your workspaces (BAUTA_STUDIO_OIDC_HOSTED_DOMAINS), and Entra ID's xms_edov vouches for an email.
  • Two-factor sign-in for passwords, with any authenticator app (TOTP), set up from a QR code on a new Account page, with ten one-time recovery codes. BAUTA_STUDIO_REQUIRE_2FA requires it of admins (the default once single sign-on is on) or of everyone. Secrets are encrypted with a key in secret.key, or where BAUTA_STUDIO_SECRET_KEY_FILE says; each code is taken once, and wrong ones are throttled per account. An admin resets it for someone who lost their app.
  • Changing your own password on the Account page, given the current one; wrong ones count as failed sign-ins, and your other sessions end. An admin sets someone's password on the Users page.
  • bauta studio set-password, the way back in for a locked-out admin, from the server's shell; --reset-2fa also turns off two-factor sign-in.
  • BAUTA_STUDIO_SESSION_HOURS sets how long a password session lasts.
  • A new sign-in ends the session the browser had.
  • The studio extra installs httpx and PyJWT for single sign-on, and pyotp, segno and cryptography for two-factor sign-in.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • The documentation is shorter and easier to scan: every guide and reference page is rewritten, keeping every setting, limit and breaking change.

docs.title: 0.2.11 — 2026-11-21
docs.text: The native masker no longer crashes Studio, a --forever run's manifest lists what it masked, DuckDB connections are locked down, MySQL upserts drop the deprecated VALUES(), and a dozen smaller fixes. No mask changes, though dateShift writes some ISO text back closer to how it came.

docs.title: Breaking
docs.text:
• A DuckDB connection's queries reach no file outside its database. DuckDB's SQL could read and write any file the process can, attach databases and load extensions, so a query in the jobs files, one edited in Studio included, could reach the machine as bauta's account. Set options: {enable_external_access: true} where queries are meant to read files.
  • DuckDB must be 1.5.1 or later: 1.5.0 refused its own write-ahead log once file access was off.
  • A readOnly DuckDB connection opens its file read-only, so DuckDB refuses writes too: a sourceQuery such as DELETE ... RETURNING emptied the table it read.
  • A relative ${file:...} is read beside the file that names it, as every other path in a file is, not from the working directory, where cron and a shell found different files.
  • MySQL must be 8.0.19 or later. An upsert names its new row AS bauta_new instead of reading VALUES(column), deprecated since 8.0.20; an older server is refused as it connects. (MySQL 8.0 left support in April 2026.) MariaDB, which has no row alias, is unchanged.
  • Studio refuses an edit naming a masking strategy from a module the jobs files don't already use, as it refuses a transform: naming one imports its module, which ran before the check. BAUTA_STUDIO_TRANSFORM_MODULES allows a module for both.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• The native masker crashed the process when a thread other than the main one loaded it first (Studio's first masked request, or an orchestrator's threaded tasks). It allocates through mimalloc 2 now, at the same speed. Every bauta-rs since 0.1.3 was affected.
  • A --forever run's manifest lists what its cycles masked. It was written once, at the end, from the last (usually idle) cycle, so it listed no job. It is now written as each cycle that ran a job ends, and an idle cycle leaves it as it was.
  • A signal between --forever cycles stops the run there, rather than starting one more cycle that marked every due job skipped.
  • A --forever cycle with nothing due logs at debug, not two lines every cycleSleepSeconds all day.
  • Run state in the layout from before watermarks no longer fails every run on its missing maskingKeys section.
  • verify-references checks an undeclared key on a table named for a reserved word, such as order, which failed as a syntax error.
  • A manifest kept in a table whose name needs quoting reads back; its content was read from the name unquoted.
  • clear holds the run lock, so it can't empty a table a run of the same jobs is loading.
  • Scrubbing a driver's message takes time in proportion to it, not quadratic: 16,000 names took over a minute.
  • bauta reports its own version, from bauta/_version.py, which pyproject.toml now reads too. An editable install reported the version it was installed at, in manifests and bauta --version, and accepted an older native masker as matching.
  • dateShift keeps ISO text as written but for its date: .5 came back as .500000 and Z as +00:00, and on Python 3.10 neither could be read, failing the job.
  • --accept-key-change checks an Iceberg upsert's key (its targetKey or identifier fields) as it does a table's primary key, where it only warned.
  • Studio:
  • Reuses the loaded configuration until one of its files changes, where every request re-read and re-validated it: a fifth of a second for 500 masked jobs.
  • A job measured, or a database checked, before 200 other checks no longer shows as never measured or checked.
  • An edit spanning several files, as accepting discovery's proposals makes, is written whole or not at all.
  • A run started before a restart no longer shows as running because another process took its id.
  • A finished run no longer lingers as a zombie process until its page is opened.
  • Two admins demoting each other at once can no longer leave no admin.
  • A jobs file is on disk before it replaces the old one, and the data directory, run logs and backups are readable by Studio's account alone.
  • A failed benchmark's message is scrubbed.
  • The web app says what went wrong when a proxy answers in Studio's place.

docs.title: 0.2.10 — 2026-11-16
docs.text: redact masks natively, five to fifteen times as fast, and in linear time in Python. No mask changes.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • The native masker covers redact, five to fifteen times as fast on one thread and spread over maskingThreads: notes a third of which hold an identifier mask at 0.6 microseconds each, not 8.6. It finds exactly what Python finds, checked by the vectors and by 20,000 generated texts under four policies. Non-ASCII text and a policy's own patterns are still masked in Python.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • redact in Python takes time in proportion to a long run of digits or letters, not quadratic: 50,000 digits took three seconds. The email search now starts only where the text holds an @.

docs.title: 0.2.9 — 2026-11-10
docs.text: Jobs can read tables of files, Studio's failures keep values out of its logs, and its tables upgrade in place. No mask changes.

docs.title: Breaking
docs.text:
• Studio refuses an edit that starts calling a transform from a module the jobs files don't already use (bauta's own aside): a transform is any callable in any module, so os:system could run commands as Studio's account. Allow modules with BAUTA_STUDIO_TRANSFORM_MODULES, or add the transform where the file is managed.
  • Studio's sign-in limit counts by email and address together, with wider limits by each. Behind a proxy on another machine, name it in --forwarded-allow-ips, or every sign-in counts as the proxy's.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Files as a source. A job can name a files connection as its sourceConnection and query its Parquet, CSV or JSON Lines with SQL, locally or in S3, Google Cloud Storage or Azure, with the same streaming, masking, watermarks and partitions as a database. An overwrite job's table reads as its newest snapshot, a table's columns are those of all its files, and CSV is read as text, so a zip code keeps its leading zeros. The query reaches nothing outside the root. The files extra now installs DuckDB.
  • readOnly on a files connection, as on a database.
  • Studio's tables upgrade in place with Alembic, which the studio extra now installs. A database from 0.2.7 is recognized and kept.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Studio no longer writes a value a driver quoted into its activity or server log. A scheduled check's failure was kept raw, and an unhandled failure written out by the server as it stood; both are scrubbed now.
  • Editing in Studio works where include reaches outside the configuration directory: every edit was refused. An edit is now checked in place rather than in a copy of the directory, and two edits at once can't both pass the check that the file is as it was read.
  • Studio's sign-in can't be used to lock an owner out from elsewhere, or to fill its memory, and checks at most four passwords at once.
  • Two requests archiving the same manifest at once no longer fail one of them.
  • Studio removes expired sessions as it starts.
  • Studio's sign-in page names the right command for the first account, bauta studio create-user.
  • A benchmark interrupted by a restart is marked failed, rather than staying running and disabling its job's Measure button for good. A job is measured once at a time, at most two at once.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • A release runs all of CI first, real databases included, and publishes nothing if it fails. CI builds and tests Studio's web app, and the dependency audit and Dependabot cover it.

docs.title: 0.2.7 — 2026-10-17
docs.text: bauta Studio: a web console a team runs on its own infrastructure, in the same package and licence. Sign in to watch runs, start, rerun and cancel them, prove the copy safe and hand a reviewer its evidence, review new columns, build subsets, and edit jobs, each change validated and recorded. The CLI gains what Studio is built on and is otherwise unchanged: bauta status, one run id from a cycle's first log line to its history and manifest, and bauta.project. Nothing breaking; no mask changes.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• bauta Studio: pip install "bauta[studio]", then bauta studio serve. Viewers, operators and admins sign in to watch runs as they go; start, rerun and cancel them; see the schedule and stale jobs; read each job's trend; check coverage, the audit and every manifest, and download a run's evidence; accept discover's proposals; build a subset; measure a job; compare two runs; and edit the jobs files as text or a form. It runs bauta run as cron does, under the same lock, checks coverage, the audit, discovery and references nightly, and never shows a key, a password or a table's value. See Studio.
  • Project, a configuration directory as the command reads it, for a program built on bauta: Project.load() reads and validates the configuration and knows where state is kept, and validationProblems(), dryRunProblems(), audit() and coverage() return what those commands find, as data. The commands use it themselves. See a configuration directory.
  • bauta status: what's running now, and where each job stands: waiting, running since when, or completed, failed or skipped with its rows or error. While a cycle runs, run keeps a small file beside its lock; one left by a process that's gone shows as ended without finishing. From Python, Project.running() reads them, and runDataJobs(onProgress=...) is told each change as a RunProgress. See what's running now.
  • A cycle's run id is made as it starts (RunResult.runId), and is the same in history, a manifest table, the manifest's new runId, status and the Starting cycle log line. After run --job, each manifest entry records its own run. See what it records.
  • status shows the rows each running job has written so far, about once a second (RunProgress.rows).
  • For a program built on bauta: Project.drift(), verifyReferences() and schedule(), as discover --update, verify-references and jobs give them; bauta.generate.subset.draftSubset(), with row counts by subsetCountQuery(); and bauta.generate.schema.createStageTable(). See the Python API.

docs.title: 0.2.6 — 2026-10-07
docs.text: Closes ways a copy could leak, lose rows or lock readers out without an error. MySQL and MariaDB no longer merge a row into another sharing a unique value; a JSON document's names, birth dates and addresses are masked by what their keys say; microdegree coordinates are moved, not left as they were; an append that fails while publishing takes back what it published; an Oracle swap killed between renames is put right; and a swapped table keeps its grants and indexes every run. requireEncryption and readOnly make the rest failures rather than log lines. coverage stops counting a table a query only mentions, and a run of small jobs is about eight times faster. Read Breaking first: masks change for some JSON fields, and some coordinates and upserts that loaded before are refused.

docs.title: Breaking
docs.text:
• Masks change inside a JSON document under keys that name personal data, where a json policy sets no otherwise. Such a value (under name, dob, address, phone, ssn and the like) is masked as that kind (fakeName, dateShift, key...) in its key's domain, not by redact, which finds only shapes and copied {"name": "Ann Smith", "dob": "1984-03-02"} as it stood. A value its key's kind can't mask fails the job, naming its path. Setting otherwise keeps the old behaviour exactly. See json.
  • coordinate refuses a value outside its axis (beyond 90° for a latitude, 180° for a longitude), naming the column. A column of microdegrees was moved as if it held degrees, by under a millimetre, and an integer column rounded it straight back, so the copy held every location exactly. The new scale option reads such columns. Values in range mask as before.
  • An upsert into MySQL or MariaDB fails, rather than overwriting another row, when a new row carries a unique value another row already has, as on the other databases. ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE fires on any unique key, so the existing row took the new row's values and the new row was never written: two people merged into one silently, as a colliding masked value would. Not retried. See how a data job moves rows.
  • email's length is at least 12, as hash's is: at 8 hex characters, two of 100,000 addresses collided more often than not. 12 is the default, so masks are unchanged. A unique email column wants length: 24 (limits).
  • A watermarked job that shuffles any column is refused where its source or target has requireMasking: an incremental chunk often holds one row, which keeps its own value.
  • coverage counts a table as covered only where a job reads rows from it (after FROM or JOIN, directly or through a CTE, derived table or UNION). A mention in a comment, string or filtering subquery counted before. A table read through a view must still be declared. See coverage.
  • discover proposes the new ip strategy for IP addresses, and key with charset: hex for MAC addresses, where it proposed hash (which an inet column refused) and keep. Policies already written are unchanged.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• The ip strategy: an address as another of its family, one-to-one, by key's permutation, so a mask is always a valid address an inet or cidr column takes. keepPrefix keeps the leading bits. Text, PostgreSQL's address types, bytes and INET_ATON integers come back as they came. See ip.
  • discover finds IPv6 and MAC addresses by value, and MAC addresses by name.
  • statementTimeoutSeconds on a server connection, so a runaway query on production can't run for hours. Each database measures it its own way, set out in statement timeout; a job it stops isn't retried.
  • Partitions slice columns that aren't numbers (a UUID key, text, a date), by count even shares in the database's own order, the bounds bound as parameters and never logged; partitions: auto slices a UUID primary key so. See partitions.
  • schema creates the source's plain indexes on the tables --apply creates, leaving out with a note those it can't recreate and any on DuckDB.
  • synthesize keeps to CHECK constraints that list values or bound a number, and names any other it can't follow. synthesize --profile ALIAS shapes rows like the same table elsewhere (NULL rates, ranges, a small column's labels) from aggregates alone, never a personal-looking column, a key, or a label fewer than five rows share. See generate data.
  • A dependency audit in CI: pip-audit and cargo audit, on every change and weekly.
  • requireEncryption on a server connection closes any session the server doesn't report as encrypted, before a statement runs. See requiring encryption.
  • readOnly on a database connection refuses every write bauta would make there, and makes PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite sessions read-only on the server too. See read-only connections.
  • coordinate's scale, for degrees stored multiplied (1000000 for microdegrees, 10000000 for E7), which discover proposes where sampled values are too large for degrees, saying to check it.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • Jobs start in milliseconds, not a fifth of a second: they fork from a forkserver that has imported bauta once. 60 small jobs took 13.2 seconds and 11 of CPU, and take 1.6 and 0.2. Each job gets the run's environment as it stands when it starts. BAUTA_START_METHOD=spawn starts each afresh. See workers.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• {{ watermark }} may appear more than once in a sourceQuery, bound at each: such a query passed validate and failed every run. One inside a comment or string is left alone, and a query whose only placeholder is there fails validation.
  • watermarkColumn matches the query's column ignoring case, so Oracle's UPDATED_AT matches updated_at.
  • A failing passwordCommand's message drops what looks like a token, and its stdout; its stderr reached the log, history and webhooks whole.
  • A webhook post is retried once, three seconds later, after a network error, timeout, 5xx or 429.
  • synthesize generates dates to the end of the current year, not 2026-12-31.
  • Offline audit says a column renamed in sourceQuery passes it, and to gate CI with audit --connect --strict.
  • A swapped table keeps its grants and plain indexes every run, not every other run: the stage is given the target's table grants and non-unique indexes before loading, on the five server databases. One that can't be given is a warning. See how a swap works.
  • An Oracle swap killed between renames is put right by the next run, finished or undone as the tables left say, where every later run failed with ORA-00942. A job past timeoutSeconds lets its renames finish before it stops.
  • A files append failing while it moves its parts takes back what it published, and one killed meanwhile is taken back by the table's next run: 12,000 of 20,000 rows had been left visible, then appended again.
  • run --dry-run no longer logs a SQL Iceberg catalog's password from its uri, and the connection's repr leaves the uri out.

docs.title: 0.2.5 — 2026-10-06
docs.text: Know where a job's time goes, keep a copy from taking more of production than it was given, and move every value as it was. History records each job's seconds reading, masking and writing; bauta bench measures a job against its source before anything is copied; maxRowsReadPerSecond caps what jobs read from a connection. An upgrade leaving the native masker behind stops the run rather than slowing every masked job tenfold. A policy naming a column twice is refused. PostgreSQL's JSON crosses exactly; Oracle's binary doubles, SQL Server's empty binaries and DuckDB's mixed JSON load; a NaN a target can't hold fails by name; and large subsets no longer crawl on PostgreSQL. Read Breaking first. Masks change only for a MySQL or DuckDB JSON column masked with a plain strategy.

docs.title: Breaking
docs.text:
• A key given twice in one mapping of any configuration file is an error, naming both lines. YAML silently keeps the last, so actor_email: email then actor_email: keep validated, read as masked, and copied every address. A key given again over a merge (<<: *defaults) still overrides it. See the security model.
  • PostgreSQL's json and jsonb are read as their text, as the other databases return JSON, so documents cross exactly: parsed, "123" came back as 123, a bare number or string failed the job, and 12345678901234567890.123 lost digits through a float. A JSON column masked with anything but keep, json or null is decoded before masking and encoded after, so it masks as before. A transform on a kept JSON column now receives text, not a dictionary. JSON Lines writes the column as the JSON it holds, and fails the job on a value that isn't JSON.
  • A PostgreSQL JSON null stays JSON null where kept or masked with json, where it loaded as SQL NULL; a check such as doc IS NULL may count differently.
  • Masks change for a MySQL or DuckDB JSON column masked with a plain strategy (such as email on bare JSON strings): it keyed on the quoted text, so it masked unlike the same value elsewhere, and a JSON column refused the result. It is now decoded and encoded as PostgreSQL's is. keep, json and null are unchanged, as is MariaDB.
  • A NaN or infinity a target can't hold fails the load, naming the table and column: MySQL, MariaDB and SQL Server read NaN as a column name, an Oracle NUMBER refused it, and SQLite stored NaN as NULL silently. The new nullIfNotFinite transform turns them into NULL. Not retried.
  • A run with masked jobs stops before it starts where bauta-rs is another version than bauta's, and validate fails, rather than masking ten times slower with a warning, as upgrading bauta alone did. Install the matching version, or set requireNative: false (or BAUTA_REQUIRE_NATIVE=0). Where the extension was never installed or is turned off, runs go on, now saying they mask in Python. See the native masker.
  • bauta history's table has four more columns, READ, MASK, WRITE and WAITED, before ERROR; --format json gives the same four fields.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Where the time went. Every completed job records its seconds busy reading, masking, writing (with its swap or commit) and waiting on a read limit, in history and notifications (readSeconds, maskSeconds, writeSeconds, throttledSeconds), its JSON log (stages) and bauta history. The stages overlap, so the largest set the pace. A history table from 0.2.4 or earlier works without them; four columns keep them. See where the time went.
  • bauta bench reads up to --rows of each job's query from its real source, masks it as run would, writes nothing, and reports reading and masking rates and which would set the pace. See measure a job.
  • maxRowsReadPerSecond on a database connection caps what all jobs and partitions together read from it, across processes. See limiting what a job reads.
  • BAUTA_REQUIRE_NATIVE=0, as requireNative: false.
  • The nullIfNotFinite transform: NULL for a NaN or infinite float, which nullIf can't match, since NaN equals nothing.
  • From Python: masking.requiresNative, masking.nativeUnavailableReason, JobOutcome.stages and bauta.jobs.throttle.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Subset queries select a table wanted for several reasons as a UNION ALL, a branch per reason, where selections are materialized (PostgreSQL, SQLite, DuckDB), not one WHERE joining EXISTS with OR, which PostgreSQL ran by rereading the selection for every row once it outgrew work_mem: 2,000 customers of 200,000 took 18 seconds, and now 0.03. The rows are the same. See copy a subset.
  • subset proposes masking without --mask where --target has requireMasking, whose jobs would otherwise fail validation, and warns where its jobs copy every column as it is.
  • schema keeps a column's spelling and a PostgreSQL array's type between two databases of the same kind: "Order" became order, and integer[] became TEXT. Across kinds, columns fold and arrays become text as before, with a note.
  • With run --job, a manifest file gains the run's jobs rather than being replaced, under a lock, so runs of single jobs side by side don't drop each other's. What the file held must verify first; an altered one is moved aside as <name>.rejected-<time>, and one signed with a key the run can't check is kept, the run's manifest written beside it as <name>.unmerged-<time>. A manifest file is always replaced in one step. See keep a manifest.
  • json writes a number it leaves unmasked as it came, 1.10 included, not through a float. Masks are unchanged.
  • discover and audit --connect find personal data in JSON whatever else the sample holds: one null document, or a column of bare JSON strings, hid every email and SSN in the rest.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Oracle BINARY_DOUBLE and BINARY_FLOAT take NaN, the infinities and values past 1e126, which binding as NUMBER refused.
  • SQL Server takes an empty binary value, which pymssql sent as an empty varchar.
  • DuckDB takes a JSON array mixing numbers and objects, which it tried to cast to a STRUCT.
  • The README said a second run refuses to start while one is going; runs of different jobs with --job go side by side.
  • bauta --version and validate say why masking runs in Python, rather than suggesting an install that changes nothing.

docs.title: 0.2.4 — 2026-10-06
docs.text: Masked copies that leak less and stay truer to production. Driver errors in unknown formats fail closed, and DuckDB's errors and the drivers' own loggers are scrubbed. json masks identifiers held as numbers and in keys. Weak keys are refused or warned about, and append jobs are guarded against a key change. audit --connect checks kept columns and shared domains by their values. New: normalize, dateShift by a column, a coordinate strategy, larger fake-name lists that agree across columns, requireNative, partitions, a swap that keeps the target's keys, and HTML reports. Read Breaking first. Masks change only where json used to copy a value unmasked.

docs.title: Breaking
docs.text:
• DuckDB 1.5 or newer is required: every 1.4 release refuses to reload a table emptied while another connection holds a transaction, so a swap job reading and writing one file failed every third run.
  • A masking or signing key of fewer than 8 different characters is refused: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa met the length rule, and its fingerprint gave it away offline. A key estimated under 128 bits is warned about; a future release will refuse it. See keys.
  • An append job writing files or Iceberg stops the run when its masking key changed, as an upsert job does: its target holds rows masked under the old key. Remove what it wrote and run with --accept-key-change. See rotating the masking key.
  • json masks identifiers held as numbers and in object keys, under its default otherwise: a number long enough to be a phone or card number is masked as its digits and stays a number, and a document keyed by email has its keys masked. Both were copied unmasked. otherwise: keep keeps both.
  • audit --connect samples up to 1,000 rows of each query, not one, and may newly warn about kept columns that look personal and domains held differently. --sample 0 reads none.
  • A swap job whose source repeats a key now fails where the target has a primary or unique key, since the stage now gets the target's keys (see Changed). It reached the target every other run. Deduplicate in sourceQuery.
  • A driver error in an unknown format loses its quoted text before it is logged, recorded or posted. An alert matching on such text may need to match on less.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• normalize on key, fpe and hash: strip and lower make values a database compares as equal (a CHAR's padding, a case-insensitive collation) mask alike, and integer masks an id held as text as the integer it spells. See values held more than one way.
  • dateShift with shiftBy keys the shift on another column, a person's id say, so all of one person's dates move together and keep their order. See shiftBy.
  • A coordinate strategy moves a point by a keyed distance on the ground, wherever it is, where number's variance barely moved one near the equator. See coordinate.
  • lists: 2 on the fake* strategies picks from longer lists and makes the name strategies agree: a full name masks part by part as fakeFirstName and fakeLastName do, in one domain, whatever its case. matchGender: true keeps a known first name's gender. Masks without lists: 2 are unchanged. See the larger lists.
  • requireNative: true (or BAUTA_REQUIRE_NATIVE=1) stops a masked run before it starts, and fails validate, whenever the native masker isn't in use. See the native masker.
  • audit --connect questions kept columns by their values, so SELECT ssn AS ref with ref: keep no longer passes, notes kept UUIDs, and warns about a domain held as a number in one column and text or padded text in another. No sampled value appears in the report. See reviewing policies.
  • partitions: {column: id, count: 8} reads a job as that many ranges at once, each with its own connections, reader, masker and writer, all loading one table. The job succeeds only if every slice does. A masked two-million-row PostgreSQL copy ran 3.1 times as fast in four slices with the native masker; without it, slices take turns at Python's lock and gain nothing. See partitions.
  • partitions: auto chooses as each job starts: its target's primary key, and the fewest of its share of the cores, its connections' free places and one slice per 250,000 rows. A job it can't slice is read as one stream, so auto can sit under defaults. See partitions: auto.
  • audit --format html and coverage --format html: one self-contained page for a reviewer, fetching nothing, never holding a value or a key.
  • From Python: keyStrengthBits, warnIfWeakKey, requireNativeProblem, installDriverScrubbing, discovery.valueHint, log.scrubbing.scrubForeignText; and for a custom strategy, CONTEXT_OPTION, contextColumn(), maskColumnWith() and defaultDomain().

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• discover proposes null for gender, race, ethnicity, religion and nationality, special categories under GDPR, where shuffle left every real value in the table.
  • discover proposes key with charset: hex for UUIDs, which other systems may hold too, where it proposed keep.
  • discover proposes coordinate for latitudes and longitudes, where it proposed number.
  • A configuration that fails validation is reported without pydantic's error chained behind it, which quotes its input, keys and passwords included.
  • A swap gives its stage the target's primary and unique keys before loading, unnamed, so the live table has them every run; a key that can't be added is a warning.
  • audit no longer counts a difference in normalize alone as a domain masked two ways.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• DuckDB's error messages were not scrubbed: conversion, duplicate-key, foreign-key and cast errors reached logs, history and webhooks with values in them.
  • The drivers' own loggers were not scrubbed; the command and every job process now scrub each record as it is made.
  • A warning that old snapshots couldn't be removed quoted its error unscrubbed.

docs.title: 0.2.3 — 2026-09-30
docs.text: Configuration scales to hundreds of tables: jobs split across files, generated jobs sharing defaults, and discover --update when production's columns change. run --full-refresh takes deleted rows out of incremental copies. Foreign keys are read from each table's own schema, and JSON and inet columns are masked and discovered. The documentation is a website, at ribeiro11075.github.io/bauta, one copy per release. Read Breaking first: relative database paths move, and requireMasking refuses defaultStrategy: keep. No mask changes.

docs.title: Breaking
docs.text:
• A relative path in connections.yaml is relative to that file, not the working directory, as jobs.yaml's already were: a SQLite or DuckDB path, a files root, an Iceberg warehouse. A configuration written for commands started above configuration/ needs path: ../prod.db for path: prod.db.
  • A SQLite or DuckDB file that doesn't exist is an error, except for a job's target and schema --apply: a misspelled source path opened an empty database. From Python, pass Database(..., create=True) to create one.
  • --quiet leaves errors on stderr, one line each, where it left nothing (and Python then printed every traceback itself). A job's failure is reported once. Under cron, that is a mail when a run fails and none when it succeeds.
  • discover and subset write what their jobs share under defaults, and leave out built-in values. --self-contained writes every setting into every job as before.
  • bauta history heads its first column FINISHED (UTC); a script splitting the header on spaces sees one more field.
  • requireMasking refuses a defaultStrategy that copies values as they are: masking: {defaultStrategy: keep, columns: {}} satisfied it and copied everything. See requiring masking.
  • verify-references exits 1 when it checked no key but keys exist in schemas the jobs don't use, where it passed with "Checked 0 foreign key(s)". With no key declared anywhere it still succeeds.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• include in jobs.yaml merges more files of jobs and acknowledged tables, by path or glob, such as jobs.d/*.yaml, one per team. defaults reaches them all; a job or table in two files, or a pattern matching nothing, is an error; the manifest records each file's digest. See splitting the jobs across files.
  • bauta discover --update compares each masked job with what its query returns now, proposing a policy for each new column and reporting each gone one; it exits 1 on drift, for CI. --apply writes the change into each job's file, leaving every other line as it was. See keeping a policy up to date.
  • bauta run --full-refresh removes rows deleted from the source, which watermarks can't see: each incremental job loads its whole source and replaces the target, by swap or one Iceberg commit, carrying on incrementally from what it read. A job it can't refresh is refused beforehand, and audit warns of it. Schedule it within your erasure deadline; see deletes.
  • bauta schema --all-tables, with --schema, creates every table in a database.
  • Examples for Airflow and Dagster in example/orchestrators/, each with a weekly full refresh, and a demo running a task per job without either. See run from Airflow or Dagster.
  • python -m bauta, where the script isn't on PATH.
  • A json strategy masks inside a JSON document: each path fields names (contact.email, items[].card) with its own policy and domain, and everything else with otherwise, redact by default. See json.
  • discover looks inside JSON documents and proposes a json policy naming each path holding personal data, where it proposed keep.
  • A cardSecurityCode rule proposes null for CVV and similar columns, which PCI DSS forbids storing, and audit questions one kept.
  • audit --connect warns when foreign keys are declared only in schemas the jobs don't use, and notes keys a source declares that its target doesn't.
  • From Python: readJobsFile(path), validateConnectionConfiguration(raw, directory=...), Database(..., create=True), Database.getForeignKeys(schema), getForeignKeysFor(tables), foreignKeysElsewhere(schemas), and Strategy.bindKey(key).

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• run --job locks only the jobs it runs, so runs of different jobs go side by side, as an orchestrator's tasks do. The same job never runs twice at once. On Windows, which has no shared lock, they still wait for each other.
  • Jobs opening a new SQLite file at once no longer fail with "database is locked" while switching it to WAL.
  • An OSError during a run, such as a full disk, is reported as itself, not as another run holding the lock.
  • A masking key changed under many jobs is reported once, grouped by old and new fingerprint.
  • The package's Documentation link points to the website.
  • The documentation is reorganized by task: getting started, guides, reference and concepts. docs/masking.md, docs/configuration.md and docs/operations.md were split into pages under docs/guides/ and docs/reference/, so links to the old files no longer resolve.
  • Every command has a page, generated from its parser.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Foreign keys in a schema other than the connection's own were never read, so schema --apply created none, discover gave keys the wrong domain, and verify-references passed copies of orphans. Keys are now read from each table's schema on all seven databases.
  • email, digits, key, fpe and redact take a JSON document or an IP address (as psycopg returns jsonb and inet), where they failed the job.
  • discover proposes a mask for an inet address, where it proposed keep.
  • discover --update recognises a query reading a schema-qualified table, so a new foreign key gets its parent's domain.
  • audit --connect blames a target table it couldn't read, not the job's sourceQuery.
  • --schema other on Oracle looked for "other" where Oracle holds OTHER.
  • discover --help and subset named a --database flag, which is --connection.

docs.title: 0.2.2 — 2026-09-27
docs.text: Faster jobs, most of all wide masked tables and anything written to files or Iceberg: 25 masked columns on ten cores went from 78,900 rows a second to 106,100 into SQLite with maskingThreads: auto, on half the threads, and from 22.2 to 10.2 seconds a million rows into Parquet. No mask changes, and nothing is written differently.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• maskingThreads: auto masks on half the cores, not all: masking only has to keep up with reading and writing, which need cores too, and on ten cores four threads copied a wide table as fast as six or eight, and ten were slower. A number still sets exactly that many. See masking threads.
  • The native masker takes a chunk in one call, masking its columns at once rather than handing the GIL back after each, and frees its strings without holding the GIL. Values Python finishes are finished in the same order, so a refusal says the same.
  • Loading a chunk does less work in Python: the values a driver takes differently are found from each row's types in one pass, in Rust where it can, not by scanning every column.
  • Writing files and Iceberg does a fraction of the work in Python: a column of plain types goes to Arrow without checking each value, which took over half a wide table's time.
  • Reading, masking and writing overlap two chunks deep, absorbing a slow chunk on either side; a job holds four chunks rather than three.

docs.title: 0.2.1 — 2026-09-27
docs.text: Jobs can write Iceberg tables through a Glue, REST or SQL catalog, in any of the three clouds: one commit a run, upsert by key, and old snapshots' files deleted with them. Read Breaking first: pyarrow and DuckDB need newer versions. No mask changes.

docs.title: Breaking
docs.text:
• pyarrow 21 or newer for the files and duckdb extras, and DuckDB 1.4 or newer. pyarrow 21 has every Azure credential and copies of any size; DuckDB before 1.4 reported a DECIMAL without its precision.
  • From Python: bauta.files is now bauta.lake, and bauta.configuration.fileTypes is columnTypes. The connection models are in bauta.configuration.connections (still exported by bauta.configuration), and DataJobConfig.writesFiles() and targetMismatch() are replaced by targetProblems(job, connection), targetKind() and isLake().

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• An iceberg connection (pip install "bauta[iceberg]") writes Iceberg tables through pyiceberg, with no JVM, via a glue, rest or sql catalog. append and overwrite commit a run once; upsert merges by targetKey or the table's identifier fields, a commit per row group. A missing table is created; an existing one decides each column's type, and refuses a new column unless evolveSchema. Each run keeps keepSnapshots snapshots and deletes the files only older ones referenced. See Iceberg and Iceberg tables.
  • run --dry-run checks an Iceberg catalog answers and its warehouse can be written.
  • Iceberg on Azure, which pyiceberg 0.12 alone can't write.

docs.title: 0.2.0 — 2026-09-26
docs.text: Jobs can write files: a files connection is a directory, or a bucket in S3, Google Cloud Storage or Azure, of tables in Parquet, CSV or JSON Lines. No mask changes, and nothing existing changes behaviour.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• A files connection (pip install "bauta[files]") writes each job's rows as a table of files under its root: append adds a run's parts beside those already there, and overwrite publishes the whole table as a new snapshot=<run>/, keeping the newest keepSnapshots. singleFile: true writes a small table as one file. Nothing is visible until every row is written, and memory stays flat. Masking, requireMasking, retries, timeouts and audit work as for any job. See files and files as a target.
  • Each column's Parquet type is fixed before the first row group, declared in targetColumnTypes or settled by its first values, and a value that doesn't fit fails the job, naming the column, rather than being cast (pyarrow writes 1.5 into an integer column as 1).
  • S3 roots, with credentials from the AWS default chain or settings, a roleArn to assume, and an endpoint for MinIO and the like. Parts are staged and published by a copy, so a failed job leaves nothing visible. See files.
  • Google Cloud Storage and Azure roots (gs://, az://, abfss://), with each cloud's default credentials or settings.
  • CSV and JSON Lines, gzipped by default, each type spelled one way in both. See formats.
  • run --dry-run checks a files root can be written and listed.
  • A files connection is a target only, for now; commands that need a catalog refuse it.
  • From Python: FilesConnection, DatabaseConfig, InsertStrategy.APPEND and OVERWRITE, and bauta.jobs.targets.LoadTarget, of which TableTarget and FileTarget are the two kinds.

docs.title: 0.1.9 — 2026-09-26
docs.text: DuckDB joins as a source or target, and connections replace databases in the configuration: connections.yaml, sourceConnection and targetConnection, each type checked for its own settings. Copies between databases load lists, JSON, UUIDs, times and unsigned integers that failed before. Read Breaking first: every configuration needs editing. No mask changes.

docs.title: Breaking
docs.text:
• database.yaml is now connections.yaml, and sourceDatabase and targetDatabase are sourceConnection and targetConnection, in defaults: too; the old names are refused. Rename the file, then the two settings.
  • The flags follow: --databases is --connections, and --memory-database, --history-database and --manifest-database are --memory-connection and so on. A state table names its alias with connection:.
  • Each connection type takes only its own settings: SQLite and DuckDB name their file with path, Oracle no longer takes an unused database, and a setting of another type is refused rather than ignored. From Python, DatabaseConnectionConfig becomes one class per type, ConnectionConfig is their union, and connectionConfig(type=..., ...) builds one.
  • discover, subset, schema, synthesize and coverage take --connection, not --database. From Python, validateDatabaseConfiguration is validateConnectionConfiguration, and validateJobGraph takes connections=.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• DuckDB (pip install "bauta[duckdb]"), for jobs and every command. A chunk loads as one Arrow table: 50,000 rows in a tenth of a second, against 13 seconds row by row. See DuckDB.
  • maxConcurrentJobs on a connection caps the jobs using it at once, whatever workers allows; always 1 for DuckDB, which one process at a time may open.
  • A DuckDB swap of a table in a foreign key or with an index fails before renaming anything, since DuckDB refuses or mishandles those renames. DuckDB sessions run in UTC, and clear empties DuckDB tables one transaction each.
  • discover warns, masking DuckDB in place, that a table in a foreign key can't be swapped.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Lists and dictionaries load into SQLite, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle and SQL Server as JSON text, as schema maps them, where every such copy failed.
  • A UUID loads into MySQL and MariaDB, and a time of day into Oracle, as text.
  • What each Python type is sent as, for each database, is one table (bauta/database/values.py). bauta no longer registers process-wide adapters with sqlite3, and a datetime watermark keeps its microseconds on SQL Server.
  • schema maps MySQL's and MariaDB's unsigned integers to a type holding their range, where the upper half of each was refused, or became a float in SQLite.
  • An integer past 64 bits loads into SQLite as its exact text.

docs.title: 0.1.8 — 2026-09-21
docs.text: The native masker covers number, masks fpe two and a half times as fast and key a quarter faster, and spreads integer columns across threads as well as text. synthesize no longer holds every key in memory, and the docs' throughput figures come from a benchmark in the repository. No mask changes.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The native masker covers number, four to six times as fast (a 5,000-row chunk of Decimals, 22 ms to 5), repeating Python's decimal arithmetic at 60 digits and handing back what it would have to guess at.
  • Masked columns are spliced back into rows by rebuilding them from columns where that is faster (narrow tables, or a third or more masked): 7% off a typical masked chunk.
  • The native fpe is about four times as fast (4.7 µs to 1.1 a value): FF1's rounds run in machine integers wherever a half fits 64 bits. Two fpe columns among six went from 105,000 to 254,000 rows a second, faster than key.
  • The native key is 20-30% faster, its Feistel network in machine integers up to 2**128.
  • Integers cross into and out of the native masker through the C API where they fit 64 bits, where each was a Python call that held up every masking thread.
  • synthesize remembers generated keys only for a table keyed wholly by foreign keys: it held every key, 116 MiB a million rows.
  • benchmarks/masking.py measures the figures the docs quote, and fails if two copies of a policy differ. See benchmarks.
  • None of this changes a mask: the fast paths are tested against the general ones at every width, and the vectors pass on both sides of each boundary.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • A number value past 60 significant digits fails as a masking error naming its column, not as a bare decimal.InvalidOperation.

docs.title: 0.1.7 — 2026-09-21
docs.text: A watermark could leak an unmasked value; the package is reorganized into groups a newcomer can find; run-state connections are closed; and loads spend less time in Python. No mask changes.

docs.title: Breaking
docs.text:
• A watermarkColumn that defaultStrategy masks is refused, by validate and run: only named columns were checked, so such a watermark wrote its unmasked value to run state and logs.
  • Modules moved into subpackages, and the old import paths are gone: configuration, database (dialects), jobs, log, transform, masking, generate, review and cli. bauta.databaseDialects is bauta.database.dialects; bauta.builtinMasking, bauta.fakeData and bauta.fpe are bauta.masking.strategies, .fakeData and .fpe; discovery and subsets moved under bauta.generate, and the reports under bauta.review. bauta.masking.Strategy, the command and every setting are unchanged.
  • bauta exports less: exactly what API stability documents. The dialect classes and ColumnCategory come from bauta.database.dialects.
  • A MemoryBackend implements all six methods; the default for fingerprints silently turned off the key-change check.
  • The built-in transforms are bauta.transform.builtinTransforms, not bauta.builtinTransforms.
  • A native masker refusing a strategy's options raises, rather than silently masking in Python: the two are always one version, so it is a bug to report.
  • Run state from before the masking implementation was recorded logs a warning once on each masked upsert job's next run.
  • bauta.masking exports the strategies and fake-data lists itself, without the shim that found them lazily.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• PostgreSQL COPY uses psycopg's own encoders, twice as fast, storing identical rows.
  • Each chunk is checked by its distinct types, not value by value: three to five times faster.
  • A PostgreSQL upsert creates its staging table once per connection, not every chunk.
  • run --dry-run and audit --connect open one connection per alias, not one per check.
  • Whether a column is masked is decided by its strategy's PASSTHROUGH, so a custom passthrough strategy counts as keep. canonical is public in bauta.masking.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Run-state connections were never closed. A MemoryBackend has close() and works as a context manager, and every command and job closes its own.
  • A connection whose session setup failed was left open, one more each retry.
  • SIGTERM under --forever waited out cycleSleepSeconds, outliving a container's grace period; it stops within a second.
  • A SQL Server swap of a table whose name holds a single quote failed.
  • run --dry-run skipped a job's checks when another job shared the name of an alias whose check had failed.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• SECURITY.md and CONTRIBUTING.md.
  • ruff check in CI.
  • The test suite fails on a connection or file left open.
  • The tests mirror the package. See where the tests are.
  • One suite runs the operations every database must perform against all of them; the copies per database had drifted.
  • CI measures coverage across unit and integration suites, and fails below 95%.
  • GitHub Actions are pinned to commits, and Dependabot keeps them, the dev tools and the Rust crates current.

docs.title: 0.1.6 — 2026-09-20
docs.text: A misspelled setting can no longer produce an unmasked copy, coverage answers what the jobs don't cover at all, and masking is faster without any mask changing.

docs.title: Breaking
docs.text:
• An unknown field in jobs.yaml or database.yaml is an error: maskng: for masking: was dropped silently, leaving a job that read as masked and copied every column, with every check passing. validate names each, offline. Top-level x- keys are still allowed, for YAML anchors.
  • audit reports every unmasked job, as a warning, or an error when its columns look personal; it was silent unless another job masked the same source. A reviewed job declares unmasked: true.
  • --accept-key-change is refused for an upsert whose policy masks the target's primary key: new keys made it insert a second generation of rows, sometimes over other rows, which verify-references passed. Use bauta clear, then run again; see rotating the masking key.
  • BoundMasking.apply refuses rows wider than its policy, whose extra columns it ignored.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• bauta coverage lists every table in a source database and what the jobs do with it, exiting 1 on any NOT COVERED, so CI fails when production gains a table. See coverage.
  • acknowledged in jobs.yaml records the tables left out on purpose, and why. See acknowledged.
  • requireMasking on an alias refuses any job reading or writing it unmasked, at validate, whatever the job says. See requiring masking.
  • unmasked: true on a job says it was reviewed and copies as it stands.
  • defaults in jobs.yaml supplies what every job would repeat, the masking key included but never a policy's columns. See defaults.
  • discover --all-tables, with --schema, proposes for every table.
  • --mask-keys on discover and subset --mask proposes key for numeric surrogate keys too, in each relationship's shared domain. See propose a policy.
  • Database.listTables(), for base tables on every database.
  • Runbooks for rotating the masking key, after a failed cycle and one production, several environments.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• active, chunkSize and workers have defaults (true, 5000, 1). insertStrategy stays required: a wrong one gives wrong data, not an error.
  • run --dry-run compares the column counts it prints, so a target that gained a column fails there, not at the next scheduled run.
  • A connection error names what it tried to reach, resolved, never the password.
  • audit --connect resolves every job's columns, an unmasked job's included.
  • The starter configuration uses defaults: and drops empty and Oracle-only fields.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
None of this changes a mask: the reference vectors pass, in Python and natively.

  • A job with no transforms no longer copies every chunk twice: 3.5 ms saved per 10,000 rows, on nearly every job.
  • A masking policy reads and rewrites only the columns it masks: one masked column of 30 went from 18.3 to 6.1 ms a 10,000-row chunk.
  • dateShift derives each day's shift once, not per row: 32.0 to 4.3 ms per 10,000 rows.
  • The checks each dialect made before a load are one pass: 35.5 to 19.7 ms a chunk into SQL Server.
  • PostgreSQL's bulk load looks up each value's spelling by exact type: 100.7 to 77.9 ms a 30-column chunk.
  • Run state in a table reuses one connection per process, not one per read and write.
  • bauta history reads from the end of the file rather than parsing it all.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• State tables whose names need quoting were written right and read back unquoted.
  • bauta/masking.py and bauta/builtinMasking.py no longer import each other.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text: • proposeTable's unused primaryKeys parameter.

docs.title: Breaking
docs.text:
• charset: hex is case-sensitive, so its masks change. Masked case-insensitively, aB12cd34 and ab12cd34 shared a mask and two keys could merge. key keeps each character's case; fpe masks both cases in one alphabet, so its masks may mix cases. Re-mask copies that must match earlier ones.
  • Table names are quoted into the statements a run builds, as column names were, so a name means a table, not SQL: an Oracle database link (orders@remote) must become a view or a table. See how names are written.
  • dateShift is keyed on the day, so timestamp masks change. Keyed on the whole value, a day's rows scattered across the month, and a DATE and a TIMESTAMP of one day disagreed. Dates and ISO date text mask as before; re-mask copies whose timestamps must match earlier ones.
  • SQLite connections enforce declared foreign keys, as other databases do, so a load breaking one, or emptying a referenced table, fails. Add PRAGMA foreign_keys=OFF to a job's preTargetAdhocQueries where it must load such rows.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• bauta verify-references counts, per foreign key on the loaded tables, the rows pointing at nothing, from the target's keys and its sources'. Counts only; exits 1 on any orphan. See checking the copy's references.
  • audit --connect warns about a job copying part of a referenced table that its referencing job doesn't match, a job that can load before the table it references, a swap of a table that declares foreign keys, and keys whose two ends are both shuffled; and reports an error for a swap of a table a foreign key references. See tables that reference each other and how a swap works.
  • The partial-copy check recognises LIMIT, TOP, FETCH FIRST and joins, as well as WHERE and watermarks.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• schema maps TIME into Oracle as VARCHAR2(32 CHAR), wide enough for MySQL's day-long values.
  • The cycle message from schema, synthesize and clear no longer offers --no-foreign-keys, which only schema has.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• A table whose name must be written in quotes was unusable: catalog lookups bound the quotes too, so it seemed to have no columns or key. Names are now unquoted for lookups and quoted into statements, by every command. See how names are written.
  • A decimal lost digits in a SQLite copy, since schema's DECIMAL(38,10) has numeric affinity. A decimal is now created as TEXT; recreate older tables to hold exact values.
  • A MySQL TIME was corrupted or refused wherever it was copied, being a duration. It is written as [-]HH:MM:SS[.ffffff], and a value no TIME column holds is refused.
  • schema couldn't tell MySQL's INT UNSIGNED from INT, halving its range silently; unsigned types are now read and noted.
  • Two tables sharing a generated job name became one job (orders and Orders, or one name in two schemas); names are now distinct.
  • A sourceQuery returning fewer columns than its target failed with a driver message naming nothing; it now says what each side has.
  • An upsert into a target without a primary key wrote first and refused after; the target is checked before anything is written.
  • A PostgreSQL json or jsonb column couldn't be copied: psycopg refused to write back the dict it read.
  • A load a masked value overflowed blamed the column; it now names the likely mask and what to do. See key.
  • An Oracle swap could lose the stage table for good when a rename was blocked; a failed rename now undoes the others.
  • A SQLite swap repointed every view on the target at the stage, which the next run emptied; views now keep naming the target.
  • A postTargetAdhocQuery failing after a swap reported 0 rows moved; it now reports the rows the target holds.
  • A run killed outright left its jobs running, beside the next run, which the dead run's free lock let start; a job now ends when its run does. See workers.
  • A name longer than the target keeps loaded whatever table shared its first 63 characters, since databases truncate silently; such a name is now refused.
  • A SQL Server swap of a bracketed name built a temporary name its parser refused.
  • schema copied constraint names verbatim, which collide on MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle and SQL Server; they are now made unique.
  • schema emitted foreign keys to unique columns it hadn't made unique; it now copies those constraints.
  • schema mixed Oracle's upper-case catalog names with the names typed; every table is created as it was asked for.
  • schema was silent about several lossy conversions it documents; it notes them now.
  • synthesize repeated its values on a second run; generators continue from the rows already there, and a refused row is reported as a SynthesisError.
  • digits copied a value unmasked when its keeps covered every digit; such a value now fails the job.
  • A masked column could be the watermark, leaking its value into run state and logs; validate refuses it.
  • Foreign keys into another schema were reported without it, so checks matched a same-named table elsewhere; parents are now named schema.table.
  • On SQL Server, foreign keys outside the login's default schema were invisible.
  • Oracle dropped every timestamp's fraction of a second, binding datetimes as DATE.
  • Oracle returned every scaled NUMBER as a float, losing digits; they are Decimal now.
  • SQL Server truncated timestamps to milliseconds; they are sent as text.
  • SQL Server converted whole columns of a chunk to one type, rounding exact values; such chunks load row by row.
  • A Decimal watermark was written to a run-state file as a float, skipping rows; it is written exactly.
  • Masking in place left the unmasked original in the stage table after the swap; the stage is emptied now.
  • On Oracle, foreign keys were read from the login's schema, not currentSchema.

docs.text: • bauta --version prints the version and which masker a run would use.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The built-in strategies moved to bauta/builtinMasking.py, and the fake-data lists to bauta/fakeData.py; old import paths still worked.
  • bauta audit no longer offers --memory flags it never read.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Masking on several cores, set by maskingThreads (1, a number, or auto) or BAUTA_MASKING_THREADS, with identical results for any count. See masking threads.
  • The native masker covers the fake* strategies, from the lists Python hands it.
  • The native masker remembers masks across chunks for key, fpe and fake*, and allocates through mimalloc.
  • The native-masking demo compares Python and Rust, and one core against all of them.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• A 25-column masked table runs at about 73,000 rows a second on ten cores, from 18,000. See speed.
  • The documentation was made consistent, and every figure re-measured.

docs.title: Breaking
docs.text:
• bauta init is removed. Copy example/starter/configuration/ instead.
  • Prometheus metrics are removed (--metrics, --metrics-push, writeMetricsFile, pushMetrics); take the flags out of scripts. History in a table covers alerting; see run history.
  • PostgreSQL uses psycopg 3 (3.2.10 or newer), not psycopg2, so bauta[postgresql] installs without a compiler.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• memory, history and manifest in jobs.yaml, each a file or a table, with flags to override them.
  • Manifests in a table, read back by bauta verify-manifest, or --run RUN_ID for an earlier one.
  • discovery.yaml: rules of your own for recognising personal data, ahead of the built-in ones.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • The built-in discovery rules moved to bauta/builtinDiscovery.py.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• bauta-rs, the native masker, on PyPI: pip install "bauta[native]", with wheels for Linux and macOS.
  • bauta uses bauta-rs only at its own version, and masks in Python, with a warning, beside any other.
  • bauta init, which wrote a starter configuration (removed in 0.1.2).

docs.title: 0.1.0 — 2026-09-18
docs.text: The first release on PyPI: masking, discovery, subsets, synthetic data, audit, sealed manifests, incremental loads and a dependency graph, across Oracle, SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Thank you for helping. docs/project/development.md is the full guide to the tests, the native masker and releases; this page is what to know before opening a pull request.

docs.title: Setting up
docs.text:
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[all,dev]"
pytest              # no servers needed
(cd studio/web && npm install && npm test && npm run build)   # Studio's web app, only to serve it
ruff check
mypy

Anything that touches SQL, a driver or a name should also pass the integration suite, against the databases in docker-compose.yml:

docker compose up -d --wait
pytest -m integration

docs.title: Where things are
docs.text:
Path What it holds bauta/configuration/ reading and validating the YAML: the models in models.py and connections.py, ${NAME} and passwordCommand in environment.py bauta/database/ one connection's streaming and loading in connection.py, what a swap does beyond loading in maintenance.py; what differs between databases in dialects/, one module each bauta/lake/ files and Iceberg tables: column types in columns.py and columnar.py, each format in formats.py, each cloud in stores.py, the targets in target.py and iceberg.py, reading files in source.py bauta/jobs/ the cycle in runner.py, each job's process in workers.py, its chunk pipeline in pipeline.py, the key-change checks in keys.py; run state in memory.py, history and manifests in reporting.py bauta/masking/ the keyed hash, Strategy and masking plans in core.py, the built-in strategies in strategies/, one module a kind bauta/transform/ per-column transforms, applied before masking, and the built-in ones bauta/generate/ discover, subset, schema and synthesize: what is built from a live schema bauta/review/ audit, coverage and verify-references: reports that move no data bauta/log/ logging, and scrubbing values out of every message bauta/cli/ the bauta command, one module per group of subcommands bauta/project.py a configuration directory and its checks, as the commands and Studio share them bauta/studio/, studio/ Studio: its server and API, and its React web app (studio/web/), built into bauta/studio/static mask-rs/ the optional native masker, in Rust; see its README example/ runnable demos and a starter configuration; see its README

Their tests are in the same place under tests/: tests/jobs/ for bauta/jobs/, and so on. Tests against real databases are in tests/integration/; see where the tests are.

docs.title: What a change needs
docs.text:
• A test that fails without it. Name it for the behaviour, and say in its docstring what used to go wrong.
  • Docs, if behaviour changes. Every configuration field and flag is documented; tests/repository/test_documentation.py checks the links. After changing a flag, run python website/commands.py to regenerate the command pages. See the documentation site.
  • A changelog entry under Unreleased in CHANGELOG.md, breaking changes first.
  • Masking changes go to Python first. Python is the reference implementation; port the change to mask-rs/, then regenerate the vectors (python3 mask-rs/generate_vectors.py). A change that alters any mask is a breaking change.

docs.title: Style
docs.text:
Follow the code around you: camelCase names and str.format. ruff check covers errors, not style; there is no formatter to run.

Documentation in the code follows one pattern, so a reader always knows where to look:

  • Every file opens with what it is for: a docstring in Python, //! in Rust, a // block in TypeScript.
  • Every function and class says what it does, in a docstring under its definition (/// or /** */ above it in Rust and TypeScript). Write it as prose -- what it returns or does, what it raises -- and add the why where the code can't show it, including what went wrong before. Tests are the exception: a test's name says what it checks, so only its module and helpers need one.
  • Constants sit together at the top of a file, after the imports, with one comment block above them naming each that needs explaining: # NAME: what it is for. Not a comment above each constant.
  • Inline comments are for logic that would surprise a careful reader. What a comment would only restate, the code already says.
